subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE RIVER    STATEMENT ON REQUEST FOR SEPARATE TRAFFIC LANES

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE RIVER    STATEMENT ON REQUEST FOR SEPARATE TRAFFIC LANES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday last, on the orders of the day, the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) asked if I had taken cognizance of a press report of a statement made by a member of the Canadian board of marine underwriters to the effect that separate traffic lanes for upbound and down-bound traffic should be provided on the St. Lawrence river. The hon. member also asked if I would comment on the suggestion.
The report was brought to my attention, and the opinions I received from my departmental officials led me to believe the incidence of accidents on the St. Lawrence is not excessive in relation to those occurring in comparable waters in other parts of the world. I was rather interested to note, too, that the press report in question stated a relatively small percentage of the accidents were directly attributable to the width of the channel. The department is at present carrying out a dredging program which is aimed at widening the existing channel to 800 feet, generally speaking, and this program involves an expenditure of more than $3 million each year. It is proposed to complete this program and determine the traffic potentialities of this widened channel before planning additional channels.

subtopic: REPORTED
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Transport. Is the minister aware of the reports that are current in my riding in regard to the Laurentides division that 35 to 40 men are to be laid oil from the Canadian National Railways on next January 1 in order to change its sections from seven miles for three employees as at present to 12 miles for four employees in the future, in spite of the numerous curves and other troubles of this railway crossing a hilly country?

speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: REPORTED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the hon. member for his courtesy in giving me notice of his intention to ask this question. It was delivered to my office just as the house opened this afternoon, so naturally I have not had a chance to look into the specific details he has mentioned. However, I think I can answer his question in answering a question put to me by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and similar questions raised by other hon. members of this house during the past few days. I would have replied to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre several days ago but I have been waiting until he returned to the house.
The question asked by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre on October 29, as reported at page 504 of Hansard of that date, was in the following words:
-is the Minister of Transport aware of the reports that are current in Winnipeg that 34 men are to be laid off from the Canadian National shops at Transcona each month between now and June, together with eight men to be laid off each month from the Fort Rouge shops? What steps is the government taking to prevent these lay-offs?
I brought the hon. member's question to the attention of the management of the Canadian National Railways, who advise that the principle must be recognized that the normal environment of the railway industry is such that the level of its working force must rise and fall under the influence of many factors. For example, in the early spring and through the period of good weather work is carried out on roadbeds, bridges, ballasting, tie renewals, re-lay of rail, construction of spurs, sidings, new branch lines, signalling facilities, buildings, and so on. In the winter months, of course, most of these activities practically come to a standstill, but there are then certain labour needs 
which arise out of winter operations in the form of snow and ice clearance, flooding, and the general hazards of difficult weather conditions.
The railway must adjust also the fluctuating demands for its services in the transport of goods and people, and it is obvious that as traffic declines there will be adjustments in railway needs for employees involved. The Canadian National traffic, in common with all other railroads on this continent, is suffering a sharp decline. Canadian National Railways traffic volume is currently running at a rate 15 per cent below that of last year. When traffic declines there is a lessened demand for output of repairs to locomotives and car equipment.
The impact of technological development has a very definite effect upon employee requirements. This will be apparent in the current dieselization program, but it should be realized that it spreads into other forms of mechanization which affect the categories of employees required by the railway. In this connection the Canadian National has done its utmost to deal with necessary adjustments in a considerate manner. It is not a question only of the actual numerical demand for employees but also the fact that a need for new types of skills and experience arises while other types are no longer required. Canadian National has taken very active steps to provide training and to give opportunities to employees to acquire the skills they need to meet these new requirements.
In the face of the present traffic situation, certain adjustments are necessary. While the present forecasts show a sharp decline and thus reduce immediate work requirements, the trends are being kept under close survey so that as soon as an improvement becomes apparent steps can be taken to keep work output to the needs of traffic.
I should say also that management, sensitive to hardships caused by reductions in staff, is not being guided solely by strict economic considerations, and is making every effort to program the work so that the impact of the serious traffic decline on employee levels may be cushioned as much as possible, and every effort is being made to find alternative employment for those who may be affected. The general level of employees in the first eight months of this year for the Canadian National Railway system is down by less than 1 per cent as compared with the same period last year.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE AND ALLOWABLE INCOME

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Friday, November 1, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Monteith-Mr. Cour-temanche in the chair:
That* it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Disabled Persons Act to increase to fifty-five dollars per month the maximum amount of allowance in respect of which payments may be made to the provinces under the provisions of that act, to provide, subject to regulations, for payments in respect of certain additional persons Who are patients in institutions, and to increase the total amount of allowable income, inclusive of allowance, by one hundred and twenty dollars a year in the case of an unmarried person and two hundred and forty dollars a year in the case of a married person.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE AND ALLOWABLE INCOME
speechtext:
When the hour of five o'clock arrived on Friday and Your Honour asked if the resolution carried, I suggested that I had one or two observations to make and therefore did not desire it to carry at that time. Let me emphasize that my action did not in any sense result from a desire to hold up action with respect to the resolution.
The resolution itself, Mr. Chairman, makes provision for three things. It goes without saying that since a good many of us in this house have pressed for these very things over the years, we do intend to support them. Ever since the Disabled Persons Act became law of course we tried to impress upon the previous government that the allowance provided was inadequate, particularly in the light of the constant increase in the cost of living. The provision of $55 a month now brings the allowance in line with the allowance under the Old Age Security Act, the Old Age Assistance Act and the proposed change in the Blind Persons Act. This is as it should be, even though I would once more emphasize that we feel that the sum of $55 could be increased still further.
We are pleased, Mr. Chairman, to find that certain disabled persons previously precluded from benefits under this act are now to enjoy certain of these benefits. I make specific reference, of course, to disabled persons who are inmates of infirmaries, homes for the aged, as well as inmates of institutions for the care of incurables. It could never be understood why those persons should have been more or less singled out and why they should have had a complete ban placed upon them so far as this act is concerned. We are therefore very pleased to find that the government has at least gone this far.
In making a statement to the house the other day the minister did refer to the inmates of two other types of institutions, those in tuberculosis sanatoria and in mental

institutions. I do not intend to debate these two specific subjects at this time. The minister did say that if help is to be given to the provinces then probably it should be done in another way. All I am going to say at this time is that I hope the federal government is giving serious consideration to granting further assistance to the provinces to enable them to meet these great burdens which they have to meet, namely that of providing adequate care and treatment for the inmates of mental institutions and tuberculosis sanatoria.
This measure also provides that the ceiling on allowable income, including pensions, shall be raised as was the case with the other pieces of legislation to which we have given consideration up to this point. Those things I have mentioned as being the changes in this proposed legislation are good. I have no hesitation in saying that. However, I am still troubled about one or two other things. Before going directly to those things may I just refer for a moment to one or two things stated by the former minister of national health and welfare when speaking on Friday.
The hon. member for Essex East referred to the election of 1953 and he said something like this. He said there had been no real public discussion of disabled persons pensions during that election, and in fact he left the impression that actually, even after the election of 1953, little thought or consideration was being given by the public to this question of our disabled citizens. Of course, the former minister is sometimes given to, shall I say in all kindness, modest exaggeration. This was at least modest exaggeration, because both inside and outside of this house prior to 1953 this subject was being keenly and actively debated.
I think that fact arose in part from two things. The Ontario government was the first provincial government in Canada to introduce legislation according certain benefits to our disabled citizens. Alberta followed reasonably closely on the heels of Ontario. Until 1953 I believe those were the only two provinces in Canada with legislation that provided benefits to our disabled citizens. I do not know, of course, as to the fact but I rather fancy it would be quite fair to say that when the legislation came down here, it came down substantially as a consequence of public pressure and-this is point No. 2-the realization that Conservative Ontario and Social Credit Alberta were maybe getting too much credit from the citizens of this country and maybe it was necessary to do something about that matter. But regardless of the cause, we were happy to see that legislation brought into the House of Commons.
On Friday the former minister of national health and welfare said those restrictive

regulations respecting eligibility for disabled pensions resulted from insistence on the part of at least one province that they be left as rigid as they turned out to be. He said "the province" and I can only take it, of course, that he meant Ontario. In my own province of Alberta this is what we discovered when the federal legislation became operative. It had the effect of excluding 50 per cent of those in the province of Alberta who had been qualifying for disabled persons pensions under our provincial legislation.
The consequence of that rigid test of eligibility is this. My province of Alberta has been forced to carry two disabled persons acts, let us say, on its shoulders. They are partners under the federal act and they pay their full share of the cost. In addition they are maintaining the act which they had prior to the passage in this house of the disabled persons legislation. Under it they are not only carrying those who qualified prior to the date of this legislation, but they are maintaining it as an instrument under which many of our citizens in Alberta who cannot qualify under the federal act will not be barred from pensions resulting from disability.
I think serious consideration should be given right now to modifying the regulations, or at the least the interpretation of the regulations, under which we ascertain whether or not a person is disabled. I have seen some rather tragic cases. One of the most tragic I have witnessed is this. Here is a person who, on the basis of the best possible medical advice, is totally disabled at the present moment and may be so disabled for three or four years. Under a strict interpretation of the regulations-and they are being interpreted in this way by many provinces-such persons are not permitted to qualify for disabled pensions because they cannot meet the requirements of the word "permanent". In the case to which I refer, which was nothing but illustrative, there was reason to believe that person might become fit again in a matter of three or four years. But during that period when persons could not qualify for benefits, because of their inability to work and because of the extremely heavy costs which were involved they found themselves completely crippled financially.
I proceed now to point No. 2. I ran into a case like this only within the last six weeks. Here is a case where I presume most doctors would say to themselves "hopeless". However, the patient may live for a matter of two or three years. The doctors do not like to admit that it is hopeless-and I do not blame them and I am not criticizing them for that-and they do not care to fill out a medical statement that the patient's condition is permanent because of the disastrous effect that might have upon the patient. I
Disabled Persons Act
refer specifically to certain cancer cases. I think the Minister of National Health and Welfare might give some rather serious consideration to that particular aspect of this matter.
I looked through Hansard covering the sittings of last year, and I found that in answer to questions the former minister repeatedly asserted that a new definition, if we may put it that way, had been placed before the provinces. However, I could not find in Hansard any reference-at least by the time the House of Commons was dissolved last spring-which would lead me to believe that the ten provinces had signified agreement.

speechtext: I dealt with that matter in my comments on Friday.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE AND ALLOWABLE INCOME
speechtext:
I shall come to that matter. What I say is that upon examination of Hansard for last session I could not find anything to indicate that the ten provinces had signified agreement. However, I noted that the former minister, the hon. member for Essex East, on Friday, as reported at page 685 of Hansard, stated as follows:
I understand that the definition of disability as liberalized, as modified in the spring, has now been accepted by all of the provinces and possibly when we reach discussion of the bill the minister will give us further particulars on that score.
I hope that all the provinces have agreed upon a more liberalized definition. I also trust that when the bill is before the house for consideration the minister will indicate our current position with respect to that matter. I know, of course, that it would not be possible for the federal Minister of National Health and Welfare probably to hit upon an interpretation, let us say, of that eligibility section and impose it upon the provinces. I realize full well that they have a right to a say, inasmuch as they pay part of the cost, and that certainly agreement should be reached among them before it is done. However, I make this suggestion, and in saying this I am talking to the provinces as much as to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. I hope they have finally reached the stage where they are prepared to eliminate, once and for all, the unfairness which exists under that particular section or aspect of our disability pensions act.
I listened on Friday while the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bryce) was speaking. I have no criticism to offer with regard to what he said. In fact my eyes popped open and so did my ears when he referred to the fact that certain persons in his province who are presently in receipt of pensions had started to work or had tried to go to work and the pension was discontinued. Then, of course, when they found they could not carry on they tried to get the pension back. Well, there are some provinces in this country

Disabled Persons Act
where if the applicant or pensioner shows any sign whatsoever of being able to work, then his pension is discontinued, even though he may never endeavour to go out to work. In Manitoba the interpretation of the eligibility section is probably much less severe than in certain other parts of the country because, as I say, I know full well that persons like that could not even qualify in certain sections of the country.
I do not desire to take up any more of the time of the house now, although I feel very keenly about the matters I have raised, and particularly as I emphasized previously about this definition of disablement. I trust we may have a correction there before too long.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE AND ALLOWABLE INCOME
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, most of the comments which I intended to make were covered by the hon. member for Selkirk on Friday last, and I do not wish to delay this house by repeating what he said at that time. The cost of this legislation is borne partly by the federal government and partly by the provincial government and it is our duty, as members of this parliament, to do everything in our powers to see that every one, as far as we can manage it, is treated in the same way and with the same degree of fairness. I therefore wish to support the pleas of all hon. members of this house who have asked for a relaxing of the regulations and for more uniformity in the administration of this legislation.
The hon. member for Selkirk put his finger on one of the weak points of this legislation when he pointed out that although this law is enacted by the federal parliament it is administered by the provincial governments. The same thing applies, of course, to some of the other social welfare legislation. I do not think any law has raised hopes higher and dashed them lower than the bill relating to the resolution now under consideration. The main act is called the Disabled Persons Act. Its very title raises the hopes of thousands of disabled people who will never be able to benefit under this act as it is now administered.
What is a disabled person? I think the ordinary person regards himself as disabled when his physical condition prevents him from earning a living or having any earning power whatsoever. However, according to the regulations under this bill a person can hardly qualify if he is able to move. I have many constituents in my riding who in my opinion should be able to benefit from this legislation, but their applications have never been successful. I have seen patients with very serious heart conditions who have been given the very best medical advice that they are not able to work and should not try to work, but their applications have been unsuccess-
ful. I know of persons who are suffering from paralytic strokes. Some of them cannot dress themselves or even feed themselves without assistance, yet these people are unable to qualify under this act as it is now administered in my province. The same applies to people suffering from hypertension, severe blood pressure and other ailments. The definition of disability seems to include a concept of totality and permanence. A person has to be totally disabled and he has to be permanently disabled before he can qualify.
Now, how can we tell whether a person is going to be permanently disabled? The fact that he is deprived of his earning power for a year is enough to put him in a very embarrassing situation even if he does manage to exist on charity for several more years.
The eligibility of an applicant, as I understand it, is decided by a board who have no personal knowledge whatsoever of the patient, yet in some cases the recommendation of the family doctor or the visiting doctor is disregarded. I think we must endeavour to overcome these difficulties to make sure that no matter in what part of Canada a person lives he should come under exactly the same regulations and definitions. The same machinery should be employed to ensure that the same interpretation of the regulations will be applied to each case.
I was interested in the figures which the minister quoted on Friday as to the increased number of people per year who might qualify under this act. I think he mentioned that the expected increase would be around
7,000	persons annually. I find it difficult to understand why the increase would be constant when the population is always expanding. I would expect that if the increase in the first year were 7,000, in the next year it might be 7,200 and in the following year 7,500 and so on in some form of arithmetical progression. I rather suspect that this constant figure arises from the fact that this bill is administered by the provinces and is therefore in some way related to the provincial budget. The province can only afford to budget a certain amount for the benefits of this act; consequently they tend every year to restrict the provincial beneficiaries to their budget allotment.
I would like the minister when he replies to give any information he may have on this matter. The minister stated on Friday that he has not yet had any time to examine the regulations in order to determine whether they need any modification to bring them in line with what is fair and equitable. I urge him now to try in every possible way to bring about as quickly as possible a conference on this matter between the provincial departments with a view to taking whatever steps

are necessary to relax these regulations, which restrict the benefits of the bill to such a small number of people that it almost defeats the purpose and intention of the legislation itself.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE AND ALLOWABLE INCOME
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I cannot add a great deal to what has already been said on certain aspects of the resolution before us, but I do want to add my word to the views which have been expressed in this debate. I can remember that when this matter was first introduced, and again when it was brought up last year, I told the then minister of national health and welfare that the regulations were such that it was very difficult to bring a disabled person within the scope of the act. That situation has not changed. Whether under the Liberals or under the Conservatives the act still remains in such a form that it is most difficult to find a complete definition and interpretation of a disabled person.
As far as I am concerned, in my own riding and in my own province I have found it impossible to bring a person under the provisions of this act unless he is completely immobile. It has been my experience that if a person has the power to dress himself or crawl to the toilet he is not considered as disabled under this act. That has been my experience in my own riding and in all cases which have been brought to my attention in British Columbia.
Before I came down to attend this house I learned of a man living two blocks from my own home who had suffered a back injury with the result that he could not stand. He had also lost a leg, and that I know as a fact because he was in hospital two years ago, at the same time I was. As I say, he cannot stand because of his back injury, and he has lost a leg. He can move-into a wheelchair-but under the act-and this I know because I took the matter up personally-he is not eligible to benefit from this pension scheme because he is able to move.
Every day he has to go out to try and sell artificial flowers and leather goods in order to live. I say again, as I said last year and the year before, that something is definitely wrong with the regulations at present laid down defining whether or not a man is eligible as a disabled person. I have heard the Minister of National Health and Welfare speaking in the last few weeks about the regulations being a matter for both the federal and provincial authorities. The administration is a provincial responsibility, it is true, but the regulations are decided upon jointly by both the provincial and the federal authorities. The federal government pays the greater part of the cost of these
Disabled Persons Act
benefits, and I believe, therefore, the federal government has the right to say something about the interpretation which should be placed on the regulations and the spirit in which they should be applied. I know I am repeating myself, but I say, that the interpretation and the administration of the regulations regarding disabled persons pensions combine to form one of the most dirty and vicious things in the administration of Canada. That is according to my own knowledge of what occurs in British Columbia.
Unfortunately to a great extent this is because of the medical board, which has a great deal of authority in making recommendations and whose members are apparently more interested in drawing money than they are in discovering and investigating the situation of persons applying for relief under the act. That is my impression as far as I know the situation in British Columbia. Surely, Mr. Chairman, the spirit and intent of the Disabled Persons Act is not that a man has to be completely crippled and unable to move before he can receive any benefit? Surely the intention is that if a man can do something for himself-if he cannot earn a living but is going to try, nevertheless-he should be entitled to receive assistance? But that is not the attitude as I have known it so far.
Thus while supporting the increase being made in the allowance I should like to ask the minister, not that he pass the buck to the provincial authorities who have the responsibility of administration but that he should recognize that it is by a joint arrangement between the provincial and the federal authorities that these regulations and interpretations are decided upon. I ask him to consider that there may be a more humanitarian approach to this subject of disabled persons than the one prevailling now, and I ask also that he should authorize a review of the cases which have been raised during the past year. I am convinced, by reference to those cases that I know, that a great many applicants have been refused the benefit which it was intended by this parliament, one year and two years ago, that they should receive. They have been denied that right because of the present interpretation which decides whether or not a person is disabled. Surely there are other definitions of a disabled person than one based on his ability to move. A person who is crippled but who tries to help himself should also be capable of coming within this category.
I ask the minister to bear this in mind and, if he wishes, I will be glad to give him particulars of a number of cases.

I have not, like the hon. members of the larger groups in this house, the advantage to have gone from one side to the other, following the last elections on June 10 of this year. On the other hand, it may therefore be easier for me to keep the position I took in the past on various projects submitted to this house including the Disabled Persons Act which the present resolution seeks to amend in a commendable way. I believe it is fair to raise the amount of the disabled persons allowance by $9 a month, and better still, perhaps to raise the income ceiling for eligibility, because this will increase the number of beneficiaries.
However, I deplore that the age limit has not been reduced from 18 to 16 years. I made a request to this effect on two or three occasions in the past, and I repeat it to-day, in order to point out more particularly the serious drawback which does not allow any indigent disabled person to receive an allowance between the ages of 16 when he ceases to receive the family allowance, and 18, when he begins to receive the assistance to the disabled.
This is a condition which should be corrected. Indeed, how are disabled persons deprived of income going to live between the ages of 16 and 18 if they are from poor families accustomed to receiving at least the small monthly amount of $8 for their upkeep and who suddenly will receive no assistance whatsoever, at a time when the cost of their care is substantially increasing?
I want also to point out, without taking up too much time-as I have done in preceding years-that in certain cases of serious illness or disability at birth or in the months or years just following birth, the disability pension should apply from that date. In a certain number of instances-and this is

according to my humble medical experience -the financial assistance which such benefit would give might enable parents to have medical care for their children, who would become normal beings, or, at least be able to look after their own needs in later life.
What considerable advantage this would be from the purely humanitarian and social point of view, with which the financial angle can never compete.
Finally, in my humble opinion, this resolution should have announced a new rewording of the definition of disability. It is all very well and good to say that all the provinces were in agreement with the federal government in this connection. I know, however, and all the hon. members probably know also, that there are still, at least in the constituency of Beauce, which is of particular interest to me, many poor people who are unable to earn their living or that of their family, due to illness or disability and who cannot get such pension.
I can only repeat here what I have already explained more fully-and these will be my closing remarks-that the physical or mental possibility or impossibility of earning one's living, in the case of poor people, should be the yardstick for the granting of a pension. (Text):

Mr. Chairman, I have one or two comments I should like to make at this time. I note in the resolution that apart from the increase in the amount of money available the objections to the act which were expressed in previous years have not been met. I refer specifically to the matter brought to the attention of the minister by several hon. members who have spoken on the resolution, that is the restrictive regulations governing eligibility under the act. I would have hoped the government would have seen fit at this time to make the necessary changes. We had every right to expect changes would be made because when the minister and his colleagues were sitting in opposition they had some extremely uncomplimentary things to say about the act.
One of my good friends who sat very close to me on this side of the house during the last parliament summed it up very neatly on January 16, 1956 when he spoke on the address in reply to the speech from the throne. At that time the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska expressed his attitude toward the

Disabled Persons Act, as reported at page 174 of Hansard of that date, in these words:
[DOT]-entitlement is realized only to the totally and permanently disabled. In other words, you have to be unconscious to get it, unconscious to keep it, and unless you walk about toting a coffin under your arm, you cannot draw that pension.
That is what a prominent Conservative had to say about this legislation just a little over a year ago and equally caustic comments were made by other hon. members of that party when they sat in opposition. The hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska went on to say:
If that pension plan is supposed to help the disabled, should not the government recognize that the pension should be paid to anyone unable through illness to earn a living at his ordinary trade or occupation? You may say that, to a certain extent, it comes under provincial jurisdiction but every government and every Canadian knows that the Liberal government has the upper hand when it comes to administration and regulations regarding disability pensions.
That was the point of view put forward in the 1956 session by this member of the Conservative party.
I am sure every hon. member of this house has received a number of letters from constituents complaining about the regulations under this act. The reason I rose to my feet this afternoon is because I received this morning a pathetic letter from a constituent of mine who has been the breadwinner in her family for a number of years due to the disability of her husband. She was anxiously looking forward to some change in the regulations which would at long last permit her husband to draw a pension under the terms of this act but, as has already been noted, the government has not seen fit to propose the necessary changes. There is still time for this to be done and I would simply like to join with my colleague, the hon. member for Vancouver East, in urging the minister to give very serious consideration at this session to bringing about changes in the regulations in order to enable many thousands of Canadians who are disabled and who, as the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska pointed out on a former occasion, have every right to receive some assistance under this act.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this order of business was announced on Friday evening. We have had a lengthy and, on the whole, a very constructive discussion of the resolution preceding the introduction of this old age security bill. In that debate nearly everything was said that needs to be said in explanation of the purpose of the bill.
The amendments proposed are simple and clear-cut and require little explanation. It is proposed to raise the amount of the old age security benefit from $46 to $55 monthly and to reduce the residence requirement from 20 to 10 years.
I have already given in my earlier statement to the committee an estimate of the annual cost involved in putting these changes into effect-$92 million annually for the $9 increase from $46 to $55 and $3.5 million for the reduction in the residence requirement from 20 to 10 years. This last mentioned amendment is expected to result in the first twelve months in the admission of some 5,000 persons to our pension rolls who are not eligible at the present time.
In addition to these two important changes, we propose to amend the act so as to permit pensioners to absent themselves from Canada for as long as six months in any calendar year without loss of benefit. The purpose of this is to grant to pensioners a greater freedom of movement than is accorded to them under existing legislation. The estimated cost of this amendment cannot be established very accurately but will certainly not be very great. It may perhaps amount to as much as half a million dollars annually. It is proposed that the three amendments be effective as of November 1, 1957.
I might point out that beginning with the cheques which went out for the month of October we have adopted a new administrative procedure which will advance the monthly mailing date by two days and result in old age security beneficiaries receiving their cheques without fail before the end of the month.
I have listened attentively to all that has been said in the course of the debate on the resolution preceding the bill and, with one possible exception, the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. LaCroix), who

Old Age Security Act
made it clear that he was opposed to the reduction from 20 to 10 years in the residence period, everyone else in the house seemed to be ready, in fact, eager to vote for the government's proposals.
So far as the remarks of the former minister are concerned I should like first of all to thank him for announcing that he and his party will support this legislation. I thank him also for his friendly reference to myself. I must confess that I was a little disappointed in the length of time he devoted to events of the distant past, events, I suppose, which everyone but the hon. member has pretty well forgotten after 30 years of more important happenings.
My hon. friend made reference to the proposed reduction in the residence requirement from 20 to 10 years. I believe he agrees with this proposal. It is true that the 1950 parliamentary committee recommended a 20-year residence period for old age security and consideration of 15 years for old age assistance. It is equally true that in 1950 some of the provinces expressed reluctance to accept a lower residence requirement for old age assistance than for old age security, but the government is not proposing a lower requirement for old age assistance than for old age security. It is proposing a uniform reduction for each from 20 to 10 years.
My hon. friend made reference to adjustments necessitated by the rising costs of living. The present adjustment in the old age benefit level is itself an adjustment to meet the rising cost of living. There is no doubt whatsoever in my mind that if the cost of living continues to spiral in the future as it has in the past further adjustments will be necessary. This has been the experience with benefit levels ever since 1927. That is precisely why I said in my opening statement that we did not consider that there was anything final or sacred about the amount of $55 that is now proposed.
I do not suggest, Mr. Speaker, that we have succeeded completely in pleasing everybody. Many members have suggested that in certain respects we have not gone far enough and others that we have gone too far. The official opposition seems to speak with divided voices on this question. For example, the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency, as I have already pointed out, is opposed to the reduction in the residence requirement from 20 to 10 years. His colleague, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill), thinks it should be reduced to five, while the last-mentioned member's former cabinet colleague, the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Sinclair), considers that 10 years is just about right and that

if we were to lower the residence requirement to five years, as suggested by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, we would encourage an influx of aged persons from other lands to Canada.
While I do not share entirely the fears expressed on this point by the hon. member for Coast-Capilano, I agree with him that a 10 year residence provision seems to be a wise and sound requirement in all the present circumstances. This represents, I believe, a reasonable middle of the road position between two extremes. We have felt that a 20-year residence requirement was a reactionary and unfair provision. Equally, in my opinion, a residence period of only five years would be premature and unwise at this time, while it would be nothing else than rash and risky, even irresponsible, to suggest, as I understand the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Patterson) did the other night, that we should eventually dispense with a residence period altogether.
I have noted also, Mr. Speaker, a number of suggestions from different quarters of the house, chiefly from C.C.F. and Social Credit members, that we should abolish altogether the restrictions on the length of temporary absences from Canada. The member for Fraser Valley wants us to pay an old age security benefit to pensioners in any country of the world. In this way, he says, our senior citizens will become ambassadors of good will for Canada. The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) demanded that I have the decency to tell the house why we did not intend to abolish the provision limiting the length of absences from Canada.
Our thinking with respect to this question of absences from Canada is very much the same as on the score of residence. We seek a prudent, middle course. We consider the present provisions much too restrictive. On the other hand, we do not consider that we have a proven case for a complete abolition of the requirement that pensioners, to be eligible, must continue to live at least a portion of the time in Canada. This is tied up with a number of questions such as, for example, the extent to which our present system is, in fact, a contributory one or, instead, based on general or even earmarked taxation. In my opinion our system is neither completely contributory nor completely noncontributory, and for this reason I believe we should move carefully and slowly in this matter until we know exactly what the consequences will be.
In addition to this I should point out that the demands of those who argue that we should continue payments to pensioners living outside of Canada run counter to the

demands that we further reduce the residence requirement. Is it seriously suggested that we should reduce the residence requirement to 10 and then perhaps to five and then why not to four, three, two or one years? There is no particular reason for stopping at five. Is it also suggested that we should at the present time agree that once a pension is awarded it carry a life entitlement, no matter where the pensioner goes to live? Surely these two proposals, when carried to their logical extremes, cancel each other out and become sheer irresponsibility. We could reach a ridiculous situation where a person could move to Canada at 69 and leave at 70 carrying with him a pension for life paid for by the Canadian taxpayers.
We cannot, in my opinion, go too far in either of these directions without jeopardizing the soundness of the scheme. That is why we propose to follow the prudent middle course, which is what the people of this nation would expect of our administration.
Last Friday, Mr. Speaker, in replying to some questions put by the hon. member for St. Antoine-Westmount (Mr. Marler), I stated that the increase in old age security
Old Age Security Act
benefit now proposed is in our judgment not only a fair and reasonable increase but it also keeps pace with the rise in the cost of living and in national productivity that has occurred since the commencement of old age security. The hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) suggested that I might table statistical data bearing on this point. I am glad to do so at this time. With the permission of the house, I should like to place on Hansard two tables, as follows: One, a tabulation showing changes in the consumer price index since 1927, changes in the maximum amount of pension payable since 1927; and changes in the purchasing power value of the pension payable each year since 1927, all based on 1949 as equal to 100; two, a tabulation showing the total amount paid out in old age pensions each year since 1927 in relation to the gross national product each year. Have I permission, Mr. Speaker?

My point is, rather, that the probable figure in which we are interested lies somewhere between the two figures I have given.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that I have now dealt with most of the specific questions that were raised in the course of the previous debate at the resolution stage. I have only one point to make in conclusion. We have heard suggestions during this debate from different quarters of the house that the pension should range all the way from $75 to $100 to $200. I do not profess to know very much about-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not going to try to cover all the ground which has been covered by the minister's statement on second reading. I should like, however, to go back to some of the points that were raised in the discussion in committee during the resolution stage, and to preface my remarks by expressing regret that I was not able to remain in the committee on Friday to listen to the minister's answers to some of the questions which I had put to him. I do not want to spend an undue amount of time now in going back over this same ground, but I should like to emphasize two points which I made during discussion in committee. These points were with regard to the terms of the pledges given by the present Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) in connection with old age security.
When I read the minister's remarks on Friday with regard to this aspect of the question I thought he had made a very valiant effort to justify the position which he had taken, but that surely he did not consider the measure with which we are dealing met the two points I raised the other day and which were firmly promised to the Canadian electors during the campaign in May and June. I might express these two points briefly by saying, first of all, that the amount of the pension was to be adjusted to the rising cost of living, if it continued. I think I should reiterate the quotation which I gave to the committee earlier, because I think it is quite clear from the speech that was given that by no stretch of the imagination could it be said this bill implements that pledge to the Canadian electors. I should like to put the quotation on Hansard again, and it reads as follows:
We intend, this September, to call together parliament and there and then fix a fair and reasonable amount for the old age pensioners, indeed for the other pensioners,-
It is this second part to which I should like to draw attention.
-and also make provision for a formula whereby due allowance will be made in the future for the rising cost of living, provided that it continues.
It is quite obvious, Mr. Speaker, that regardless of what the minister has said, and regardless of the relation which the amount of $55 bears to the previous pension or bears to the national productivity or any other
Old Age Security Act
figure, there is nothing whatever in tnis bill that would satisfy the pledge of the Prime Minister that provision would be made for a formula whereby due allowance would be made in the future for the rising cost of living. Regardless of the efforts of the minister, which were very laudable and understandable, the plain fact does remain that the bill contains no such formula as was specifically promised in the federal election broadcast of May 22, 1957. Nor does it meet the other point which forms part of the pledge given by the Prime Minister in May at Toronto, that was that the amount of the pension would be geared to the national productivity.
Surely there can be no suggestion for a moment that the bill contains anything that gears the amount of the pension, $55, to the national productivity. Quite obviously the amount of the pension, the aggregate cost of the pension in any year, has a relationship to the gross national product or to the gross national product for 1956, but the word "gear" in the minds of Canadians would stand for some process embodied in the legislation by which changes in the gross national product would be reflected in a movement, preferably upward, of the amount of the pension.
I want merely to emphasize the fact that the bill which we are now discussing contains no provision whatever to link the present amount of the pension with future changes in the gross national product or with national productivity, if I might use the words of the Prime Minister when he spoke in Toronto.
The second point I want to make is that the minister, in dealing with the bill on second reading and indeed in his discussion of the measure in the committee stage when he closed the debate, carefully stayed away from dealing with what I consider to be one of the major problems arising in connection with this measure. I refer to the effect which it has upon the total cost of social security in Canada and the effect that cost may have on expenditures for national defence.
The other day I pointed out that so far as I could tell the total cost of social security has now reached the point where of the tax dollar that is retained by the federal government, after remitting to the provinces their share of the taxes which the federal government collects on their behalf and remits under the terms of the tax-sharing agreement, 27 cents is actually devoted to social security. In other words, the cost has reached a substantial amount. I pointed out that for the last fiscal year the estimated cost of social security-that is to say of

Old Age Security Act
health, welfare and social security-had reached the rather substantial total of $1,050 million. I pointed out that changes in the number of recipients, or growth in the number of those who are entitled to receive old age security, family allowances and the other social security measures which have been under consideration, would account for the addition of another $30 million expressed in round figures.
I pointed out also that in the earlier part of this year 1957 changes in the various social security measures had added $108 million to the annual cost. The minister has told us again this afternoon that the cost of this measure will add another $96 million to that total. During the discussion of some of these other measures he told us that there will be a further addition of approximately $13 million. We can therefore see that the total cost of social security is not far away from $1,300 million, if we think in terms of what the cost to the Canadian taxpaper would have been had all these measures taken effect on May 1, 1957.
Mr. Speaker, I do not want at this stage -and perhaps it is not appropriate that I should do so-to deal with the other questions which fit in with this question of the cost of social security and the additional costs that this measure involves. I think I should merely sum up the views I expressed the other day by repeating what I said then, namely that while I think Canadians all across the country welcome any advance in social security measures that can be supported and sustained by the Canadian economy, I am sure they would view with considerable disquiet advances in social security that were going to be made at the expense of national security. I had hoped that the minister would be able to deal with this point when he closed the debate at the committee stage. Perhaps he will have an opportunity of doing so later on in the present debate. I think it is a point of considerable importance and one with which he should deal specifically.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I think the minister should tell us what the government proposes to do in connection with the fuller investigation of old age security which the Prime Minister promised when he spoke at Anti-gonish, Nova Scotia early in the campaign. At that time he expressed quite clearly the opinion that we were dealing with a contributory system. His opinion does not . seem to be entirely shared by the minister himself. If I might just quote one sentence from the report in the Globe and Mail of May 1, 
1957, of the Antigonish meeting, I think it would show the views of the Prime Minister on the subject:
The U.S. program, he said, is contributory but many Canadians forget that through two per cent each of their income tax, their sales tax and corporation tax they contribute to and pay for old age pensions.
Mr. Speaker, I shall spare the house the tedium of listening to the annual results of the old age security fund since the incep-tioin of that fund at the beginning of 1952. However, I think I should again draw to the attention of the minister a point that we raised during the committee stage, namely the effect of these new proposals; and I include not only those which are now under discussion but also those that have already taken effect as the result of changes made earlier in this year. I should like him to explain much more fully than he has done how it is intended to finance the additional cost of old age security.
We all recall that when old age security was instituted late in 1951, simultaneously there was established an account known as the old age security fund to which were to be paid two per cent of the income tax, two per cent of the sales tax and two per cent of the corporation income tax. During the early years of the fund there were deficits in the fund because the amount paid out for old age security exceeded the receipts from those three taxes. But in the current year, the year 1957-58, we had reached the point in the beginning of the year when the estimated total of old age security pensions exceeded in the estimate by only about $6 million the receipts which it was expected would go into the fund during the fiscal year 1957-58. Since then two important additions to the outgo of that fund have been made. First of all the amount of approximately $60 million resulting from the changes made at the earlier session this year, and now this further addition which we are in process of discussing and which will add a further $96 million. Hence, in a word, Mr. Speaker, we are adding some $156 million to the outgo of this fund.
I realize-as, of course, does the minister- that the whole addition is not going to be effective in this fiscal year 1957-58 because the effective date of the increases-the one voted by the previous government and the one which we are now discussing-which will be November 1, 1957, will mean that the whole burden of those increases will not be felt in the current year. But nevertheless there is added an amount of $156 million to the obligations or the outgo of the fund, and I think this house is justified in

asking the minister, either when he comes to reply at this stage of the bill or in committee, to tell us just how it is proposed to deal with what seems to be a much larger annual deficit in the old age security fund than we have known at any time in the past.
I know that in the past the deficits have represented not unsubstantial amounts which have been made good from time to time by votes of this house. But I think the minister should go further, having regard to the substantial addition or, perhaps I should say, the substantial additions made in this current year because so far as I can see the fund is going to be very much in the red unless a process of some kind is devised to make good these deficits. Is it the intention of the government to increase the amount of the taxes diverted to this fund? Is it the intention to levy a tax specially for old age security? I think the members of this house and the public of Canada generally are entitled to know how this very substantial expenditure is going to be financed.
I think it has been made perfectly clear by what has been said by my hon. friend the member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) and other members who have spoken on behalf of the official opposition that we intend to give this measure our full support and of course it is our intention to vote for the second reading of this bill.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during my years of residence or presence-I do not know which you would call it-in this house I have spoken quite a number of times on the question of old age pensions but I have not spoken previously in this debate on the resolution. I certainly
Old Age Security Act
support the bill as an improvement on previous legislation and I am not going to deal with it at length. I think my colleagues expressed our point of view very well at the resolution stage. However, I do want to make two or three comments with respect to certain aspects of this social security legislation, after listening to the minister's opening remarks and I can assure you, Mr. Speaker,
I will do so with my usual economy of language and charity of purpose.
I was interested in what the minister had to say with respect to allowing a reduction in the period of residence, yet not permitting the old age pensioner to live fulltime in some other country and still enjoy the benefits of his pension. I have listened very carefully to his explanation. I am one who thinks that the 10 years residence is very fair indeed; I think it comes in between the two extremes, the extreme of 20 years and the extreme of no-residence requirement. I think it is very fair to the newcomers in this country and to the Canadian people as a whole.
However, I have never quite been able to see why persons receiving old age security, which is largely on a contributory basis, should not receive the same privileges accorded to persons receiving other federal government pensions; for instance such persons as judges and so on. I have always thought there was a measure of injustice in that situation. This bill does improve the situation by permitting an old age pensioner to be away for what would be in effect a total of one year, if necessary, by taking six months of one year and six months of the next but I do not think this improvement meets all cases. I would suggest, that while I am in favour of the stand taken by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) consideration be given to those people on old age security who would benefit by residence in another country. I have run into a number of cases and would like to suggest to the minister that as he does not see fit to amend the legislation so as to permit a pensioner to leave Canada and enjoy his pension in any country where he wishes to live consideration be given to permitting those persons who find it necessary for health reasons to leave Canada to do so. I do urge that this first step in the right direction be given some consideration.

Mr. Speaker, I feel that the minister
in replying to a question raised by an hon. member of this house did, in fact, emphasize a weakness in this legislation. I will support the bill with only one exception. I personally will vote against the decrease from 20 to 10 years in the residence qualification, if the bill is left in its present form. I believe that I will be able to show that this particular clause has the effect of creating serious discrimination in the position of pensioners and taxpayers.
In 1949 the cost of living index was 100 and the pension $40. In September 1957 the cost of living index was 123.3 which would require a pension of $49.32 per month to be proportionate. On the basis of the cost of living index the increase to $55 would suggest an improvement in the position of pensioners over 1949.
However, a comparison of the average weekly wages and salaries of industrial workers as shown in the August 1957 publication of the dominion bureau of statistics gives a rather different picture. The average wage at May 1, 1949 was $43.10; by August 1957 it was $68.38. Comparatively the old age pension would have had to be increased

from $40 in 1949 to $63.46 in 1957. Thus it is clearly shown that $55 a month will not give pensioners their share of the rising standard of living which we have enjoyed in Canada since 1949. In fact, they will, proportionately to the general position of people in Canada, be worse off than they were in 1940. Until our old age pensions have been increased to a point where they reflect a proportionate standard of living, at least equal to that which we acknowledged in 1940, no further group should be given a pension which does not require a means test.
When the Old Age Security Act was created in 1952 it was stated that the measure would be financed by sales tax to the extent of 2 per cent on the cost of goods chargeable, 2 per cent of corporation income tax and 2 per cent of personal income tax to a maximum of $60. There is little doubt that these charges were defined to justify the removal of the means test. In turn the public feel that this particular pension is contributory, and therefore a right at the age of 70. It is probably on these grounds that the government suggests the reduction of the qualifying period. Herein lie the main injustices of the bill.
Under the provisions of this bill persons may come to Canada at the age of 60 and qualify for a pension at 70. In this short period, and at that age, they will not contribute materially through the taxes mentioned. On the other hand, a person who has lived in Canada all his life and paid taxes throughout that period can obtain a pension at 65 years of age only if he qualifies under a means test.
I note that the period of disqualification is to be increased from three to six months. This is admirable in itself, but ridiculous when related to the qualifying period. Persons may live and pay taxes for 70 years in Canada, yet lose their pensions if, even for health reasons, they find it necessary to live elsewhere for more than six months. The whole character of this reduction clause reflects adversely on the comparative position of those who have contributed so much throughout their lives, not only in taxes but in the development of the national wealth and culture of our country.
On the other hand the federal government does have a responsibility to senior citizens brought into Canada. A pension is the finest way to render assistance when there is need.
The Social Credit stand that basic pensions should be at least $60 based on their relative position as acknowledged in 1949, is fully justified. An escalator clause would be a good addition to the bill, but, if included, it should give consideration not only to the cost of
Old Age Security Act
living but also to the standard of living as reflected by the wage level or the level of national productivity.
In conclusion, I personally feel that the injustices which I have described can be easily avoided. Those who become entitled to pension by the reduction in the qualifying period should be subject to the same means test as required under the Old Age Assistance Act. Any savings thus made could be used to lessen the severity of the means test regulations for all pensioners or to improve further the position of our pensioners who find it necessary to live elsewhere than in Canada.
