Mr. Speaker, I rise only in order to give the house the few views that I have with respect to this matter. After listening to the various comments and proposals made by members in all quarters of this house, ranging from such things as a cost of living bonus or a bonus based on the gross national product to paying the pensions to people who live in other parts of the world than Canada after they are entitled to receive it, adequate hospital care, adequate housing and so on, to the question of social security legislation for our elderly citizens I think we must take an approach different from that which we have taken in the past.
Ever since the inception of old age pensions-and many hon. members of this house who have been here for some years know this far better than do I-the approach has been on this basis: What can we do which will assist these old age pensioners immediately and which also might be looked upon favourably in the country when it comes time for us to go back to the people and see whether or not they want to return us? I do not say that is done consciously nor do I say that it is the sole consideration which has been given to the old age pension structure. Nevertheless, that appears to be the attitude or the approach that we have used when these changes have been made, namely on a sort of expediency basis. I do not think it is good enough.

Before I progress any further I should like to make a comment about the suggestion as to a cost of living bonus. I know, as do other hon. members, that this suggestion was contained in the comments made during the election campaign by various members sitting on the government side of the house, but quite frankly I am pleased that they dropped it at this time and that it is not contained in the bill. To my way of thinking at the present time, if we were to adopt some sort of cost of living bonus we would be perpetrating a great crime against our old age pensioners. It is true that when the cost of living would go up, it would raise the pension itself, but by so establishing at this time a system of cost of living bonuses we would be in effect saying that the present standard of living of the old age pensioners is good enough and that it is not going to increase any more. It would be in effect saying: "You are not going to get anything better; all you are going to do is to keep up with what you are behind the present cost of living".
Quite frankly, I am of the opinion that the approach we must make to the social security legislation for old age pensioners

and we are dealing with them in this bill-must be changed. We must take some cognizance of the problems and make some effort to solve them. Whether it be done through having a study by departmental officers, a commission, or a committee, it is immaterial. We must take continual looks at these questions of health care, hospital care, adequate housing, changes in the actual amount of the pension, residence qualifications, whether you are out of Canada, and all of the many other good, sound proposals which have been made.
I hope the government will keep that thought in mind if they have not considered it already and that by doing so and establishing our approach on that basis we can generate a better feeling in society towards our elder citizens and can give them the fullest possible means for an adequate way of life in their later years.

subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I just want to say I am very much in favour of the bill under discussion. I support it mainly because it is an instrument designed to bring about a greater measure of recognition and justice for our senior citizens who have made this country great and will save many from privation and starvation.
The proposed amendments in the Old Age Security Act included in this legislation will give greater consideration to the needs of that group of Canadians which have long been neglected and which deserve better treatment from those who are the direct and indirect beneficiaries of their valuable work

and effort. It will be of some benefit to those who have as the pioneers of Canada been performing their duties under most primitive and daring conditions, making this country what it is today. It will assist those who for one reason or another could not reap the benefit of their labour. It will be helpful to those who through no fault of their own have not been able to help themselves, and it will at least compensate to some extent those who have lost the greater part of their savings through inflation.
I have mentioned these different categories which will benefit from this increase in pension for the enlightenment of those who are still confused in their own minds in that they regard any social legislation or improvement thereof as a major disaster. I repeat, those who for some unknown reason prefer individualism to Social order, and those who for selfish reasons have through manoeuvring our entire economy into a chaotic condition created inflation to the point where the buying power of the Canadian dollar is now worth less than 50 cents. This is the reason why we are here today to pass laws for increasing old age pensions to make up for these losses.
What is inflation? I think at this time we should ask ourselves this question. According to the Oxford dictionary inflation, applied to commerce and economics means "increase beyond proper limits for instance of prices". In more simple terms, if anything could be more simple, it means that inflation is created by unreasonable rising of prices from which some sections of the community benefits at the expense of the rest. The section to which our old people belong is one of those which lost the most through inflation, for rising prices mean an automatic decline in the buying dollar of the dollar; it means that many of these people who have been indirectly robbed of more than half their savings, which in many cases represented the greater part of their life's work, will once again have to be provided for by emergency measures.
It was a similar situation the other day when we were dealing with the case of the farmers. The hon. members of this house are called upon to pass laws compensating these people for their losses-these people who work hardest, saved the most and have lost the most-these are the people who followed the practice dictated by the age-old wisdom of putting aside a few dollars for a rainy day and have been caught in the squeeze between rising costs and falling value of our currency. The unbalanced condition created by inflation has reduced
Old Age Security Act
the purchasing power of their accumulated savings to less than half its original value. Many of these people have been reduced because of the dwindling value of the dollar to the point where they have become permanent wards of the government.
Most of these people were solid and thrifty citizens and did not wish to pass their remaining years in such a condition. They purchased war bonds and life insurance, contributed to pension funds and accumulated savings accounts only to find that a dollar saved in 1939 has lost half its value. They find that because of the almost 4 per cent increase in consumer prices in the last 12 months their dollars invested in government savings bonds a year ago have not brought in sufficient interest to cover the depreciation of their money. They find their self denial in accumulating savings to provide a nestegg for their old age has been in vain. They find that their total reward for their efforts is ultimate bankruptcy plus old age pensions; they find the whole process is a shameful delusion.
Even those who through their power of collective bargaining were able to keep pace with the rising cost of living have become victims of the ever-rising price spiral at their retirement. Without any means of raising their income, they stand helplessly by, watching inflation taking bigger and bigger bites out of their fixed income. Their pension cheques which could buy goods for $100 in 1949 are worth today only $83, or a loss of 17 per cent in seven years. What they could buy for a dollar a year ago now costs $1.04. This is the result of the economic crime we call inflation.
We are now called upon to save some of its victims by increased social legislation. There are to be three changes made in our old age security laws to ease the crippling effect of this inflation. First, to raise old age pensions from $46 to $55 monthly; second, to cut the period of Canadian residence required to qualify from 20 years to 10 years and, third, to lengthen from three to six months the permissible period of absence from the country in any year without loss of pension.
Adding these increased social measures to the $6 increase in old age security pensions provided for by the former administration will reimburse to a considerable extent those whose income has been largely wiped out even though it is not enough to provide very much for future losses, in which case the pension should be raised to $60 or more. One must admit that taking into account the fact that this increase is being granted by the two older parties it

Old Age Security Act
can be regarded as a somewhat remarkable achievement. They really deserve credit for this performance.
Thanks to what H. B. Mayo describes as the conscience of the country, that is the C.C.F. party, the old line parties have gradually been forced to accept the principle of social assistance to the needy. The party's founder, Mr. Woods worth, was the man who laid the cornerstone of Canadian social thinking. Since the party was formed in 1932 it has created a social consciousness in this country that no one can escape, no matter how crusty he may be. Even the old party politicians are becoming bewildered by public opinion and confused in their own thinking to the point where they are now trying to outdo each other in helping socialism, as the Ottawa Journal puts it, to come in through the back door.
Of course, there is actually nothing wrong with socialism if you look at it the right way, and as long as it is democratic. Socialism comes from the word social, and most people want to be social. Webster's dictionary defines it as a "theoretical contract by which men obtain true freedom to substitute a state of law for a state of individualism."
This makes it quite understandable why the two old parties are so anxious to comply with one of its major principles. It was interesting and at the same time amusing to listen to the former minister of national health and welfare arguing with the present Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Monteith) the other day over the matter of who is bringing in the most social legislation. But what I cannot understand is this: if they want to do it, why do they not join the C.C.F. where they could do it through the front door instead of the back? The establishment of adequate social laws has always been one of our major policy planks. But how far will it go?
Unless the government is willing to do something formidable to stop this curse of inflation which has impoverished whole sections of our society, something of this sort will have to be done to tie them to the constantly increasing cost of living. In the Financial Post of August 3 it was clearly pointed out that not only pensioners, annuitants and retired industrial wage-earners are taking a sharp drop in real income, but more and more wage and salary recipients are feeling the pinch of rising prices, and feeling it despite pay increases. Especially in those industries where white-collar workers predominate, wages tend to lag behind prices.

It is often said that increasing wages create inflation. But on page 21 of the same issue of the Financial Post, appears this statement:
Salaried workers and wage earners in service industries are either achieving small real gains or losing ground in real terms. Average weekly wages in some industries are lower in both dollar terms and real terms.
In a table contained in the September 21 issue it is clearly shown that increases in labour income are losing pace and have declined from 3.5 per cent in the first quarter of 1956 to 1.5 per cent in the first quarter of 1957, a drop of 2 per cent in one year. Who is responsible for this condition? Where is this prosperity so many people talk about? In the Financial Post of August 30 appears this statement:
In industry, all major groups have chalked up impressive increases, not only in dollar terms but also in terms of what those dollars can buy.
This is the unbalanced condition existing in our country created by inflation. On one side, rising prosperity and, on the other, decreasing income. This discriminatory process of one group being allowed for years to exploit another group has now progressed to the point where emergency laws and social legislation must be employed to save the losers from poverty and starvation. If it had not been for this economic injustice that is allowed to go on without being checked year after year we would not need to use the Canadian taxpayer's money to compensate for the losses by increased pensions.
Unless the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) has the patriotic courage to tackle inflation, which has become the core of our trouble, and resist the political pressure of selfish class interest, the increase in pension will not be of too much assistance to our senior citizens. This monster of inflation will eat it up from one end almost as fast as we can feed it with temporary stop-gap measures from the other end. If nothing more fundamental is done it will not take too long until those who depend solely on pensions will be behind again.
Those who enriched themselves in this manner will obviously resist any attempt to stop or even slow down inflation. They accuse any person or political party that attempts to stem the tide of rising prices of trying to create a recession or even a depression. They do not seem to know that any inflation, if not stopped, is automatically followed by a depression. Some of them are naive enough to suggest that a little inflation is quite all right.
When some years ago, former president Harry Truman was asked what he thought

about having just a little inflation, he replied: "You cannot have just a little inflation. Having a little inflation is like being a little pregnant."
The United States authorities as a whole seem to be much more concerned about the dangers of inflation. Apparently they have learned from the past that while people are slow in losing their confidence in money, once it is lost it is equally difficult to restore it. They seem to remember much more vividly the episode of the thirties than those who are responsible for maintaining respect for the measure of value of our own currency. This is proven by the fact that since 1947 the purchasing power of the United States dollar has declined by 20 per cent while ours has lost 29 per cent in the same time.
At the beginning of the year President Eisenhower asked congress to appoint a citizens' commission to study the nation's economy to determine where their financial system is out of date and how it can be made equal to its task.
What have our governments done? The Liberal government instituted what is called a tight money policy, consisting of restricted credit accompanied by high interest. That can perhaps be compared with putting a block of ice on a thermometer. It will lower the temperature reading, but does not end the heat wave.
The present government apparently decided to reverse this policy. Shortly after its election, the Minister of Finance announced that the tight money policy must go. I thought there could be no doubt that high interest rates would go with it but instead since that time interest rates went up by one-quarter of one per cent, and this move, to my surprise, was initiated by the Bank of Canada which is a government institution.
Mr. Speaker, the basic truth of this whole matter is that our government must either squarely face the problem of inflation and accept the policies necessary to check and curtail it, or else it will produce what former president Hoover called a hair-raising depression. It should be obvious by now to every thinking person that this merry-go-round of rising prices and increasing wages must stop. Merry-go-rounds are for children and not for intelligent adults.

subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, representing as I do a Vancouver riding, the question of increased benefits under the Old Age Security Act and the Old Age Assistance Act, is of particular concern to me. It is an undisputed fact that British Columbia has the greatest percentage of
Old Age Security Act
senior citizens of any province in the dominion and most of these citizens live on the west coast and Vancouver island because of a mild and temperate climate more suited to their years. These senior citizens pioneered this country, built up its wealth, raised and educated their families and made Canada the great nation it is today. The pension they receive is theirs by right of hard work and by right of their contributions through the various taxes levied to help defray the cost of these pensions.
The ordinary wage earner with a family finds it almost impossible to put away any money to take care of his old age. Such savings as were made during his best working period are today paid off in depreciated dollars. The senior citizen who has given his children a good education, bought a house however small, and perhaps saved a few dollars as well, has done an exceptional job for himself and this country.
The first amendment to this bill is to increase the pension to $55 a month. I was most interested when the minister informed the house the other day that this represents a 37.5 per cent increase over the $40 level which prevailed at the first of this year while by comparison the cost of living index has risen only 23 per cent since 1949 and only 5 per cent since 1952 when old age security payments commenced. At the time of the commencement of old age security payments in 1952 the gross national product was $23J billion while in 1957 it is estimated at $30.8 billion or an increase of 32.4 per cent compared to the pension increase of 37.5 per cent.
However, in assessing the value of this increase it is necessary to consider the other welfare measures which are part and parcel of the whole welfare program we are considering at this time, namely increases in payments under the Old Age Security Act, at an estimated cost of $13 million per year divided equally between the federal treasury and the provinces; increases in pensions for the blind at an estimated cost of $1 million to the federal treasury; and increases in pensions for disabled persons at a cost of $4.6 million divided evenly between the federal and provincial governments.
I wish to quote from the statement of the minister when he introduced the resolution on October 24 as reported at page 385 of Hansard of that date. I think the minister put it in a nutshell when he said:
May I add a further word, Mr. Chairman, with respect to the level of benefit that is now proposed, namely, $55 per month. We make no extravagant claims with respect to this benefit. We do not say that it is the final or perfect solution, or that there is any magic rightness about this particular

Old Age Security Act
amount. We make no extravagant claims as to the generosity of the amount we are now proposing. It is my view, rather, that we should try to measure what we are doing here not in terms of generosity but in terms of justice.
Mr. Speaker, I submit that this bill does measure what we are doing here in terms of justice. Considering all of this, I believe the increase proposed is a fair and reasonable one as it takes into account the increase in the cost of living and adds an increase over and above this for good measure. The pension has not been tied to the cost of living which could conceivably result in cutting pensions if the cost of living went down, but I am confident the government will be reviewing the pension periodically if living costs continue to rise.
I am certain that nearly all hon. members are in agreement with the second amendment which reduces the basic residence requirement from 20 to 10 years.
I would now like to say a few words about our pension arrangement as compared to plans in operation in the United States. The United States plan is carried without government assistance by means of contributions from both employer and employee. The benefits given are greater than those supplied by the Canadian old age security plan. However, it has the weakness that it helps only those workers employed in factories or other places who can be reached by the principle of deduction from pay cheques. It might well be that in the future some national scheme on a fully contributory basis could be evolved which would reach these people and provide them with a supplementary pension.
The opposition has been pointing out the increased cost to the Canadian taxpayer of this and other measures. Actually, Mr. Speaker, these measures are not inflationary in the slightest degree. Every dollar received under the provisions of this act will be spent immediately on food, shelter and other living requirements.
Hon. members speaking previously during the resolution stage have pointed out that there are many instances of pensioners not receiving any benefit from increases in their pension due to automatic increases in rental or subsistence charges leaving the pensioner with not one cent more for himself. I believe that through the administrative staff handling pensions and by pensioners reporting back such happenings publicity could be given or other steps taken which might curtail this practice.
The third amendment increases from three to six months the length of permissible temporary absence of pensioners from Canada. I think all hon. members will agree this is a

step in the right direction. It might be that later on the minister would consider setting up reciprocal regulations with other countries, particularly in respect to commonwealth countries, as the spending of pension cheques in these countries would be an aid in helping to correct the present imbalance in our foreign trade.
In conclusion, I believe that the government will have to give the lead to industry to see that first class workers are not retired both prematurely and arbitrarily. The effect of this premature retirement on the worker who continues to be fit in both mind and body and who wishes to carry on working at a job he is quite capable of doing is frequently the worst imaginable, but the social circumstances are serious too and likely to become more so. The average life span is progressively lengthening with each decade and, unless we revise our ideas, before long the rapidly growing numbers of older people who are compelled in one way or another to become dependents will constitute an enormous burden on the working population.
There is a real fear in the heart of all when they reach the middle forties or fifties that if they lose their jobs they may not be able to get another one because, and only because, of their age. We must take the leadership in educating all employers in Canada to the end that our older workers are as freely accepted as our younger workers.
The measure before us is a just one and is supported by Canadians in all age groups. The government is to be commended on the speed with which it is acting. It is doing more and in less time than any previous government has ever done.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at eight o'clock.

subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) himself has said that our old age security legislation should provide an amount which, in his words, would meet the needs of our senior citizens. In listening to the debate in the house, both at the resolution stage and at this stage of the bill, I have not heard any member, even a member from the government benches, suggest that $55 a month will meet the needs of our senior citizens. I have not heard a member from the government benches suggest that that amount, even with the provincial bonus, will meet the needs of our senior citizens.

I think, Mr. Speaker, that those needs could be met, certainly more adequately, if our old age pension legislation rested upon a fair, even-handed and just financial basis. The present old age security legislation, as we have been told many times, draws its finances from three sources, the 2 per cent of the sales tax, the 2 per cent of corporate taxation and the 2 per cent applied against income tax. It is the last 2 per cent that I want to draw attention to for the moment.
This 2 per cent is a tax applied only to the first $3,000 of taxable income. As we all know, this has meant that in the last few years a most inequitable system of taxation in that regard has existed in this country. It has meant that a man with a taxable income of $3,000 a year pays $60 into the old age security fund and a man with a taxable income of $50,000 a year pays only $60 into the fund. Or, to take an extreme case, a man with a taxable income of $100,000 per year still only pays $60 into the fund.
It is axiomatic that fair taxation laws should bear most heavily on those best able to pay. Taxation should be based upon ability to pay and it seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that the problem of financing adequate old age security would not be nearly as great as it is if only, as I say, the government would base the pension fund upon adequate and equitable taxation principles.
There is another source from which this fund should be supplemented at the present time and that, of course, is the field of capital gains, the field from which the great unearned fortunes that are being made in Canada today spring. They do not spring for the most part from earned income or salary, they spring from capital gains in speculative ventures, often a gain which results far more from the general improvement of values in the community than from any effort made by the individual concerned. Yet this vast source of fortunes is utterly untaxed in Canada today.
I would hope, Mr. Speaker, that before too long the government will consider bringing down a budget. As a freshman member of parliament I am particularly concerned to try to see the total picture, to try to see how the $95 million or so that we are proposing to add to the pension fund liabilities fits into the total picture of the revenue of Canada and the picture of how that revenue could be supplemented. I hope that will be done, together with a review of the industrial and business picture across Canada today.
But I suggest that even without seeing that total picture, which can only be presented
Old Age Security Act
in a budget, there are rich fields of taxation which should be taxed to help to provide adequate security for our senior citizens and, as I said at the beginning, I do not think that anyone can pretend that we are doing that by this legislation. So I say that the iniquitous 2 per cent application against income tax which stops at $60 and which hits the relatively poor man just as hard as it hits the rich man must be done away with. I say we must tax capital gains. I say if you evolve a taxation system which is fair, just, equitable and evenhanded you will have the funds to provide adequate old age security for our senior citizens, certainly at a basic level of $75 to which should be added the provincial bonuses.

Mr. Speaker, I have a brief word to say. I think the provision to grant six months absence in a year is very generous. The pensioner will be able to spend half his remaining life outside of Canada. Let us take a man who has not been long married and has a young family. We will say that he has come to Canada from one of the best countries in the world, Ireland. He does not see any future for himself or his family in Ireland and he says to himself, "I think I will go to the best country in the world, Canada." Out to Canada	he	comes.	What does	hefind in Canada?	He finds	all the work	he
can do and he is not only able to provide for himself and his family but is able to educate his children and save a little.
When he becomes 70 years of age he gets $46 or $55 or, as one hon. member would have it, $75. Some people like my hon. friend here would say that he should be allowed to go where he likes. I do not think he should	be	allowed	to go where	helikes. I think	he	should	be grateful	to
Canada and it is a sin of ingratitude if he wants to go back to Ireland and live there. If he wanted to go back to Ireland so badly he should have stayed there in the first place.
I think the minister certainly has been very generous in extending the period of absence to six months. When I sat on the other side of the house, Mr. Speaker, I found that no matter how generous the government was there were always those who wanted twice as much. If the minister will open his eyes he will see that situation has not changed. Some hon. members are saying that he should not have made the period six months, that he should have made it for life. I do not think he should. If a man needs a particular climate he does not have to go outside of Canada. We have all kinds of climate in Canada from the Atlantic to the

Old Age Security Act
Pacific. In Victoria you have a mild climate. In Calgary or the Rocky mountains around Banff there are the chinook winds which bring about a change in climate. If you go to Fort William you will find the climate always changing and you will get the best hockey in the world which enables you to forget yourself.
I think if a man is grateful he will want to live in the place that has treated him generously. Instead of making the period six months, I think the minister should have made it less but he can go to sleep and feel that even if he had made it twelve months there would be those who would want to make it twenty-four.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I realize that a great deal has been said about the Old Age Security Act and the amendments that are proposed. I think there has been far too much said about certain promises that were made prior to the election. In the Medicine Hat constituency the Conservative candidate, to my knowledge at least, never mentioned old age pension or old age security or old age assistance or anything of that kind. subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext:
Be that as it may, the Liberal candidate did not make any specific promises either. He made several references to common sense being used in legislation. That was all well and good, except that when I went to visit some of the old age pensioners, some of those who had to live on what they received in the form of old age security payments, it did not make sense to me that in a country such as Canada which is able to produce so abundantly all those things that are necessary for a good life, they should have to try to get along on $46 per month.
I should like to add my support to the argument advanced by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) to the effect that an increase in old age security payments would put money into the hands of people who would buy consumer goods. In that regard I should like to say that in no part of Canada do we find any shortage of consumer goods. For that reason it would appear to me that any money put into the hands of these people would not increase inflationary pressures.
During the course of this debate several members have mentioned the fact that we should try to eliminate politics from old age security and old age assistance of any kind.

I think we may as well be realistic and face the facts. Politics and political manoeuvring are part and parcel of our democratic system and so long as there are candidates representing different parties going to the people and asking for a mandate, they are certainly going to bring up matters of such importance as old age pensions or any other kind of social security. As long as we have human nature with which to deal in political elections I am certain we are going to have old age security and all social security measures brought into election campaigns, no matter how hard we strive to keep them out.
There have been suggestions also that there should be an escalator clause attached to the scale of payments under old age security legislation. I certainly go along with this idea, although I am not quite satisfied in my own mind as to whether that should be tied to the cost of living or whether it should be tied to the gross national product or to what it should be tied. In looking at this picture we must realize that if we are to be a progressive nation, then the standard of living must rise. If we tied the payments to the cost of living that would not, in fact, take care of an increased standard of living as our country may be able to provide it. While I do not have the exact formula for doing this, my feeling is we should be able to study the matter and then set up some kind of plan whereby we can make increases as the nation is able to produce the goods and services necessary to increase the standard of living.
So, Mr. Speaker, I should like to conclude by saying I support the amendment as an instalment, as a step in the right direction. I do not believe they are adequate. We in the Social Credit party advocated $60 per month basic pension. While that was considered the minimum and $55 of course falls even short of that, we cannot but support the measure because it is at least a recognition of the fact there is a need for an increase, and it is an instalment. Until such time as we can arrive at a formula that will adjust old age pensions without an act of parliament and maintain what we believe to be an acceptable standard of living for our old age pensioners, I think I will go along with the amendments as they have been stated.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my first remark would be that the more I listen to the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) the more I am certain he is misplaced and ought to be sitting on this side of the house rather than on that. We can all, of course, agree with his sentiments and they were well expressed indeed. It will

certainly come as no surprise to hon. members that I am going to support this measure. I have not been prompted to make these remarks because of the dinner recess, but rather because of the comments of one member of the C.C.F. party who suggested that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Monteith) and the former minister of that same department were gradually drifting towards a state of socialism, so much so that they might just as well become socialists. I do not think I would be remiss if I were to state to that gentleman, and to the gentleman who is doing his best to interject, that that is far from the fact although perhaps that hon. gentleman would wish that situation could occur immediately.
The hon. member for St. Antoine-West-mount (Mr. Marler) interjected some comments with which he may be surprised to find I am in some measure of agreement. He suggested or inferred that we are today looking at some substantial costs resulting from what has become, in the last half decade, a very enlarged welfare state. Perhaps one conclusion we could draw from his comments is that in looking towards the future and the extent of the social benefits in any form that any administration, regardless of the political party that may be responsible for it, can provide, consideration must be given to just how far this state can go without social welfare legislation becoming a big drain on the general economy of the country.
Having said that, Mr. Speaker, let me very quickly say that before we determine where we shall put a stop, if a stop is required, the stop should not be made at the expense of those who are least able to fend for themselves. The point that I make is that no one in this house has registered a protest, and I think rightly so, to this measure. Most hon. members have, if nothing else, indicated support to a degree based on the necessity or urgency of the measure. This is, of course, introduced as an urgent measure. I say, therefore, regardless of how we look in the future at the measures that come before this parliament, we must ask ourselves who, in regard to this legislation, can defend themselves or look after themselves best and who cannot. I believe those who have contributed to this country, be they senior citizens or veterans, have a prior claim; and that is exactly what this government is recognizing in this measure.
I think perhaps it is a regrettable commentary on our situation today that we accept the fact that we enjoy a fairly high level of prosperity and yet we see, in this and every other community, a situation in which many of our elderly citizens are being
Old Age Security Act
obliged to put up with the most distressed conditions. I think we all ask ourselves how this can occur when so many are enjoying the prosperity to which I have made reference.
I therefore say that legislators, regardless of who they may be in the future, should- as this government are doing today-give their consideration to the urgent demands of those who need it most. But certainly they must recognize the fact that other measures of social security must at some point be fully conditional on the ability of the economy in which we live to meet and be able to pay for them. I agree with the hon. member who said that we in effect must be able to recognize the fact that, unfortunately, we cannot lift off the tree all the funds that are necessary to meet these benefits that we think should be introduced in this house. But what I say-and I think this is where we differ-is that this is one of those measures which, judging by the hundreds, yes, literally thousands of letters which members have received, recognizes the seriousness of the plight of our elderly citizens who, as I say, are not enjoying anything of the benefits of our prosperity but who nevertheless suffer all the disadvantages of an inflated economy.
I believe this government should be congratulated for recognizing the urgent demand of these people who have contributed so much in the past; and because of this fact they have placed at the head of their legislative program perhaps not the most important bill that we should see but certainly one of the most urgent.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a brief word about the effect of this legislation on immigrants to this country. I have in mind, first of all, the principle of the bill which reduces to ten years the residence requirement that existed under the earlier legislation which is now being amended. I am thinking of the beneficial effect it will have on immigrants who have come here in recent years from the British isles and countries of continental Europe. I must confess that I always found it difficult-I know that my difficulties in that respect were shared by all of the hon. members on the government side of the house-to understand how it was that our predecessors in office were unable to accede to the recommendations of our party, then in opposition, made over long periods of time to do what this legislation now brings about.
From the figures that were mentioned by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Monteith) I understand that approximately 5,000 of the immigrant population

Old Age Security Act
will stand immediately to benefit. In other words, immigrants who are now 70 years of age and who came to this country during the years from 1938 to 1948 will enjoy a benefit of which they would have been deprived for another 10 years under the legislation in its unamended form. It is true that these people did not contribute to the production or the revenue of our nation except for a brief period of time, but on the other hand, neither were they the recipients of some of the costly benefits in the gift of our nation to bestow.
I have in mind one specific case in which the practical benefits which will flow from this legislation can easily be illustrated. I am thinking of a professional man from one of the countries of eastern Europe. I shall not identify him more specifically for fear of some embarrassment that he might be occasioned. He was a lawyer and in his own country he occupied a position of eminence and prestige in his profession. He enjoyed the high regard and respect of all the citizens of his country as a famed lawyer. However, because of his hostility to communism and inability to submit to its slave-like domination, he came to this country. Here he was required to live in simplicity and frugality, in circumstances far different to those to which he had been accustomed in the land of his birth. Presently he is engaged in employment which for him, because of his age, is physically exacting and indeed soon becoming impossible of performance. This citizen to whom I refer has just attained the 70th year of his life. He will be resident in this country ten years about the summertime of 1958. He is but one of many who will stand to enjoy the charitable and merciful benefits of the amendment.
In respect of one other aspect of the legislation, however, I should like to be permitted to advance merely a suggestion for the consideration of the minister and the government. It is in reference to the people referred to by the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) a moment ago namely those who choose to leave the country and who still wish to enjoy the benefits of this legislation. There are many in that category who came to this country early in their lives and who, over a period of many years, have contributed heavily to the production and the revenue of our nation. The people of whom I am thinking at the moment when I make these remarks are largely people who come from the British isles, of whom there are many in my constituency.
They came here at an early age, have engaged in many and varied occupations in this country and, as I say, have contributed

heavily to its advancement. Some of them have been here as long as 30 years and some as many as 40 years. However, their memories of the lands of St. Patrick and St. George or the lands of the shamrock and the heather are still green and they would like to go back in the declining years of their lives in order to pass the remainder of their days in those surroundings. It occurs to me that in the case of persons who fall within that particular category some exception to the present legislation might possibly be made. As I say, they have contributed heavily to the country's production and revenue. I realize that the proposal may have broader ramifications and must be considered in the light of those ramifications, but I respectfully hold out that suggestion for consideration by the minister and the government.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to add my support to those in this house who have expressed themselves as being in favour of the increase in the old age pensions. However, I suggest the proposals fall far short of the promises made during the election campaign when those candidates now on the government side said that the Conservatives would, if elected, consider extending the present old age pension system by the addition of an insurance scheme similar to that in use in the United States. That is not the purpose of the bill introduced during this session.
While we do suggest that it is still not enough it is a step toward more security for the old age pensioner. Proven statements of welfare organization issued over a year ago showed that an income of $75 per month was the bare minimum for the existence of a single person. May I say that in Saskatchewan the C.C.F. government is taking up the slack of inadequate federal old age pensions by providing supplemental allowances, hospitalization and medical services. In addition, Saskatchewan provides nursing home care to the chronically ill in provincially operated nursing homes. Over 40 old age pension home projects are now in operation in Saskatchewan for the senior citizens of our province.
Prior to the 1957 federal election campaign the senior citizens of Canada were a forgotten people. They had no means to increase their meagre pensions in the twilight of their lives despite their hard work and contributions over a period of many years. I heard one speaker in this chamber a few days ago suggest that the provincial governments are not paying their share toward the care of needy old age pensioners. Until there is a change in the fiscal policy which now

exists whereby the federal government takes 75 cents out of every tax dollar I suggest no provincial administration can do all they would like to do on behalf of their elderly people. With the remaining 25 cents out of every tax dollar paid in taxes having to be distributed between 4,600 municipal governments and 10 provincial governments it leaves much to be desired, but I suggest tonight that we get on with this legislation so that our old age pensioners will at least have the feel of a few extra dollars before the cost of living catches up with them. We have already heard that landlords have increased the rents of the old age pensioners to be effective when this increase is paid. Until our economy is planned for the benefit of the people of Canada we will continue to have this unequal condition. Let us pass this legislation immediately and with it extend our best wishes to the old age pensioners for another larger increase after the next election. We could say now that it is not much but it is the spirit that counts.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened to a great many remarks coming from your left and far right giving qualified support to this amending legislation. I do not think that simply because we sit to your right we should regard this solely as an achievement; I would much prefer tonight to think that this is a challenge and that starting from here we can go on to the point where we feel we have attended to all the needs of our senior citizens. I remember the remarks of the hon. member from Calgary South (Mr. Smith) who very forcibly pointed out that at any particular stage in the development of a country there is just so much which can go into this type of legislation. We have a serious problem if a great part of the gross national product is used in certain respects and in such a manner that it will will not produce and create further employment; then of course it is possible that the well of taxation will dry up.
I cannot help but recall being challenged on occasion at public meetings during the last eight or 10 months and being asked whether this party would approve pensions anywhere from $75 to $100 I think the most sane answer to this question is simply to say "If you were in a position where you might some day have the responsibility for fixing the amount then such estimates as are given and thrown across the floor at public meetings are the type which would have to be regarded in a very light manner."
I think that as matters now stand this legislation is doing as much in a cash way as this country can handle. I think, however that there are other things which are being done for senior citizens and other things which can be done in the future which will to a great extent alleviate some of their problems, particularly in these times of

Old Age Security Act
comparative inflation. I am thinking that perhaps as we look to the future we might give more serious thought to the problems of housing accommodation.
What can be done in this matter has been brought very forcibly before me as I have seen the efforts in this direction in my own constituency. There I saw the co-operation of three levels of government-municipal, provincial and federal-providing class A1 accommodation for senior citizens at prices they can afford to pay. I think that in future we might direct our efforts along these lines to a greater extent.
In metropolitan Toronto, as a matter of fact, I think we have to pay great credit to the present hon. member for York South (Mr. Beech) who while he was reeve of York township led the way in the construction of the Beech Hall apartments in Weston; it was at municipal level that the leadership came from. We have an example of the same type of construction in York West. There we have the West Acres apartment project. This unit was constructed by the municipality of metropolitan Toronto at an approximate cost of $800,000. It consists of eight buildings of 16 suites each, making a total of 128 suites of which 64 are bachelor suites, a total capacity of 192 elderly people.
The important part about this is the rents that are charged for this type of accommodation. The bachelor suites are $33.50 plus hydro, $1.50, and water, 75 cents, making a total of $35.75 per month, and I would like to point out that equivalent accommodation in apartments in other areas immediately adjacent to this cost between $115 and $120 a month. The double suites are $40 plus hydro, $1.50, and water 75 cents, a total of $42.50 a month.
This indicates, in this case at least, that two can live as cheaply as one. The first unit in this building project was opened on February 1 this year, and the last unit was occupied in May. There is room on this site for the possible expansion of this project by another eight buildings. A similar unit is, I understand, under construction in North York and it is expected it will be ready for occupancy, in part at least, in 1958. This building will cost in excess of $900,000 and will be identical with the unit in my own constituency except that the rents are to be $40 for bachelor suites and $50 for double apartments, including hydro and water. At present in metropolitan Toronto we have a waiting list of approximately 1200 people for these apartments.
I should like to illustrate the method of financing the West Acres project. The province of Ontario contributed $64,000 on the
TMr. Hamilton (York West).]
basis of $500 per suite under the Elderly Persons' Housing Aid Act. Metropolitan Toronto contributed $170,000 as a long-term loan with interest only payable; Central Mortgage and Housing contributed $618,350 on a 50-year mortgage arrangement. It should be pointed out here with regard to this type of assistance for elderly persons that not one cent is chargeable to the federal administration. This money is totally repayable with interest. The province makes an outright gift towards the construction; the municipality lends the money and retains at the end of the period title to the property.
In times when there are terrific demands on the government here is a method by which we can improve the lot of elderly persons and at the same time improve prospects in the building trades. I do not think the kind of co-operation I have described could be devoted to any better purpose than this. As a matter of fact I believe that with the new attitude which is being exhibited to the provinces by the government we can expect that this is a type of co-operation which, in the net result, will produce a great deal more actual comfort for our senior citizens than probably any long arguments about this legislation tonight.
I would like to say in closing that no matter whether we sit on this side of the house or the other, let us take tonight as a starting point, let us not look to the past. Let us take credit for this as an achievement but at the same time let us regard it as a challenge.

subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext:
If the
remarks we have heard, Mr. Speaker, were an indication that the hon. member for York West (Mr. Hamilton) and his party are going to recommend that something further be done for the old age pensioners in the form of housing developments which will take their income into consideration, then we will indeed be looking to the future rather than to the past. But as I have listened to the various comments which have been made about the government's proposal and the various rates of pension which have been discussed I believe that the member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) was probably quite correct when he said we were running a bingo in this regard.
Before the last election took place many years had gone by during which the old age pensioner had not been well taken care of. If the rate was not a fair one, we should have been doing something about it in those years before the $6 increase was finally granted at election time. Since that was done the cost of living has again risen. It

has continued to rise, and now we are offering the old age pensioner $55. I suggest that $55 is not sufficient to bring the pension up to the standard of living which he had in 1949 when the $40 pension was in force, and I think the amount of $75 which we regard as a suitable rate should be justified.
In recommending any increase to the old age pension I think we must develop a means by which the rate can be tied in with the cost which the pensioner has to bear, and one of the ways in which he could do that could be found in the method of financing the pensions.
We have a limitation of 2 per cent with a maximum rate of $60 making this a contributory type of pension, to an extent, and I can see no justification, and I do not think the Canadian people can see any justification, when we reach that stage of $60 why the people who have the money to pay income tax no longer have to contribute any more than the $60. So I think we have been amiss when we have not made the suggestion that we take that little bit off and make it truly contributory. Those who are more able to pay should be allowed to do so.
If we have a pension plan which we have agreed is at least partially contributory it is obvious that the contributions have been made by our senior citizens who have produced the wealth of the nation and they should have some say about what they do with the small percentage of that wealth which we give them in the form of old age pensions and old age assistance. This being the case, I say that we cannot limit these people in terms of telling them where to live and what to do with their pension.
If an aged parent wishes to take up residence with his child in another country because he has no other close connection in Canada then he should be free to do so because of the right he has established by contributing to his pension. I think we should eliminate the requirement under which people must periodically return to Canada, to check in as it were, and reestablish residence here in order to continue receiving the old age pension. I believe they establish their residence in Canada during the years they live here and build up their pensions.
There are three points in this legislation, as I see it, and I am in complete agreement with the third which reduces the residence qualification for participation in the old age pension plan.
I would think the Canadian people are going to have to and will take a look at the financing of the pension plan. There is no reason at all to believe that the cost of
Old Age Security Act
living is not going to continue to climb. We have heard no solutions from the government with regard to inflation and monetary problems in general and, as was mentioned by the previous speaker, we have heard very little from the government as to what is being done to meet the housing problem. I am glad to have heard what was said this evening because I know in my own community in Ontario the minute this pension is increased every dime of it and in some cases more is taken off for rent, food, drugs and the other commodities the pensioner has to buy.
In my constituency we have a home for aged people run on a cost basis by a church as a non-profit organization. The pension is so low that the municipality must pay $15 in addition to the pension for the inmates of the home who cannot receive financial assistance from their children, relatives or friends. In the light of the constant increase in the cost of living the increase we are now providing will be eaten up in the way the increases granted in the past have been.
It is my opinion that we have an obligation to our senior citizens to closely scrutinize the financing of our old age pension plan with a view to bringing it into line with the cost of living and through the insertion of an escalator clause or by some other means providing for increases proportionate to the increase in the cost of living so that we will not have to wait until an election is held before the old age pensioner is given a pension adequate to meet his needs.

Mr. Speaker, I just want to say a word or two with regard to Bill No. 19. Unlike hon. members in the official opposition I can express my happiness about this legislation with considerable consistency because ever since coming into this house in 1953 I have advocated increases in old age pensions. On the other hand, my hon. friends in the opposition are being most inconsistent in expressing their views. I gather from their comments that they are going to support this bill but when they formed the government and were in a position to bring in these increases all they did was bring in an increase equivalent to 20 cents a day for old age pensioners. They seem to be full of criticism now which is of course their right and duty in the opposition but it is not exactly constructive criticism. However, as long as they vote for the bill and we get the increases through this month and into the hands of the pensioners, all will be well.
The hon. member for York West (Mr. Hamilton) spoke of the Beech Hall project

Old Age Security Act
which happens to be in my constituency. We are very proud of it because it answers the need of our senior citizens for an independent and happy existence.
I am extremely pleased that the qualifying length of residence has been reduced from 20 to 10 years. There has been some criticism voiced both in the house and in the form of editorial comment across Canada about reducing the period of qualifying residence but I think we forget that the young adult immigrants who are coming to Canada bring with them their skills, trades and education. They represent no cost to Canada and we are inclined to lose sight of that fact. I have seen the figure $10,000 cited as representing what it costs Canadian taxpayers to educate one Canadian child, involving education, the baby bonus, health benefits and all these things. I believe the young immigrants who are coming to Canada will be a tremendous asset to this country. The older people who could no; qualify for the 20-year residence period in large part are the parents of these young immigrants. I believe we owe it to these new Canadians that we consider them as Canadians.
There have been many injustices under the 20-year qualification period. One example in my own constituency is that of a woman who came here from Britain as a bride. She lived here for 30 years and raised and educated four children. Just before the last war she and her husband went to England for a holiday. The war came along and all four of her children who were grown up at that time entered and fought in the Canadian forces for Canada. The woman and her husband were forced to remain in England and eventually the husband died. The woman was unable to return until 1947 and because of the hiatus of seven or eight years in her residence in this country she could not qualify for the old age pension. The present legislation will remove the possibility of that sort of injustice occurring. I feel that this is a good bill that rights many existing wrongs and I give it my wholehearted support.

Mr. Speaker, it occurs to me that I should have reserved my opening remarks on second reading for this stage of the debate. I think I answered at that time practically all the questions and arguments that had been raised in the discussion on second reading. However, I will attempt to answer one or two new angles that have been brought up.

1 would like to mention that while everybody seems definitely in favour of this bill the degree of variance ranges from one extreme to another. I would simply like to mention again the point I brought out in my opening remarks at this stage of the bill to the effect that if you carry these various conditions, such as the residence rule and permissible period of absence, to the ultimate extreme as has been suggested upon occasion you could readily create a situation wherein you would have a person coming to Canada at 69 years of age, staying one year and taking out of Canada a pension totally paid for except for one year by the Canadian taxpayers.
We believe we have reached a reasonable, sound, middle of the road course in these two provisions whereby we reduce the residence requirement from 20 to 10 years and increase the absence permissible from three to six months. We also, of course, believe that the $55 rate which we have set is the correct rate; after due consideration we believe that is the correct figure. We do not say it will meet every requirement-no. I do not think anybody could ever claim that and we do not pretend to, but what we do say is that in most cases, together with any private funds the senior citizen may have, this amount will meet the situation.
1 should like to assure the hon. member for Welland (Mr. McMillan) that any increase in pensions are always passed on directly to the beneficiary involved. There may be private retirement plans which hinge on the amount of the old age security cheque. I am not saying there are not because I do not know particularly. All I can say is that the cheque issued by the government of Canada to the pensioners is in its full amount. If there are these other situations I would say that they should be looked at and brought to the attention of the public, as the hon. member has done tonight.
The hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge), the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Hahn) and the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Maloney)-possibly there were others and if I have missed them I am sorry -have mentioned that if some pioneer Canadian citizen who has lived here all his life and has paid taxes in one form or another for years and years should at the age of 70 have to go south for his health he should be allowed to do so. I am inclined to think there is a great deal of merit in that suggestion. I certainly will be very happy to give it consideration as time goes on, but at the moment I do not see that we can do much about the matter without giving it considerable study.

Incidentally, the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne) mentioned a pro rata pension. I think that probably falls into the same category. The hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) claimed during the debate that these pensions should be made payable any place and he wondered how many had been cancelled during the period of the scheme. I may say that the total is roughly 2,500. I mentioned that earlier in my remarks.
The hon. member for St. Antoine-West-mount (Mr. Marler) seemed very concerned about where the money was going to come from for this measure. I would be happy to tell him, of course, that if the formula were being changed it would seem reasonable that an amendment should be included in the amendments at this time as the two-two-two formula is actually mentioned in the bill. But I would also refer him to section 11, subsection 3, of the Old Age Security Act, which is in these words:
If the Minister of Finance is of opinion that the amount to the credit of the old age security fund is or will be less than the amount required to pay the pensions payable under this act, he may from time to time direct that amounts be credited to the fund by way of temporary loans and the amount of such loans shall be charged to the fund by way of repayment at such time as the Minister of Finance may direct.
Subsection 4 reads:
The Minister of Finance shall annually report to parliament the temporary loans, if any, made to the fund pursuant to this section, and whether, in his opinion, the revenues of the fund are or will be sufficient in the ensuing year to meet the charges on the fund without further loans and, if it appears that the revenues will not be sufficient, he shall state what measures he recommends for the purpose of increasing the revenues of the fund.
I would suggest that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) will announce his procedure at the appropriate time. I might also point out, however, that there was a considerable surplus at the end of the last fiscal period, and when the former minister of transport suggests that we may endanger our defence effort I am positive that will not be the case and he may rest assured that indeed that will not be done.
It is a strange coincidence that the amount involved in the amendments contained in the bill approaches $110 million which is not very much more than the amount used out of last year's revenues, namely $100 million, to set up the Canada Council.

speechtext:
I should like to draw to the attention of the minister two points in connection with the drafting of the revised subsection 1 of section 5. I should point out that in the first part of this subsection provision is made for the case of a pensioner who absents himself from Canada for a period in

Old Age Security Act
excess of one month, and provision is made that payment of his pension will be suspended immediately following the payment for the month in which he so absents himself, but may be resumed when the pensioner returns.
The second part says:
-where the pensioner returns to Canada within six months from the last day of the first month in which he so absented himself from Canada, the pension upon being resumed may also be paid for the period during which he so absented himself,-
These are the words I want to draw to the attention of the minister.
-but not exceeding a total of six months in any calendar year.
Now, it seems to me to be very clear, Mr. Chairman, that what is intended by this language is that the period of absence must not for the purpose of pension exceed six months. From the language here one would almost believe that regardless of what happened the total amount of instalments that might be paid to the pensioner was not to exceed six months in any calendar year. Perhaps I have not made myself quite clear. If a pensioner absents himself for just less than six months, I take it that it is the intention that he should have his pension not only for the six months he remains in Canada but also the six months during which he is absent. However, the language almost suggests that in the event of his being away for these six months the total payments will be -I draw attention to the last line-"not exceeding a total of six months in any calendar year".
It seems to me, in reading the section that that might almost limit all of the payments the pensioner was to receive to six months, whereas I conceive it to be the intention that if his absences do not exceed six months he receives payment for the six months he was in Canada and likewise for the six months he was absent, provided he meets the other conditions of the subsection. I should like to draw the minister's attention to the wording. It seems to me that if the wording were to refer more clearly to the period it would leave room for no doubt as to what the pensioner was to receive.
whether the language expresses that intention as clearly as it ought to be expressed.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59

Well, Mr. Chairman, in some of these things I have to admit we go by what the law officers of the crown say. They are responsible for drafting this bill to meet the intentions of the government. The clause reads in part:
-six months from the last day of the first month in which he so absented himself from Canada, the pension upon being resumed may also be paid for the period during which he so absented himself, but not exceeding a total of six months in any calendar year.
The wording is somewhat changed from the previous subsection which it replaces, but at the same time I am led to believe it meets the requirements of and the intent behind the legislation. In my opinion, it seems reasonable.

subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext:

-the pension upon being resumed may also be paid for a period of such absence not exceeding three months in any calendar year.
