subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext:
I must admit that I, too, find myself a little confused. I have not got it completely clear yet, from a reading of this section, especially the latter part of it, where it says:
-the pension upon being resumed may also be paid for the period during which he so absented himself, but not exceeding a total of six months in any calendar year.
Now, would that stop a person being away October, November and December of this year, that is three months, and then being away three months in the first part of the next year because those three months would not be in the same calendar year?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext: He would have to return by March 31 next year, then he could subsequently go away again but he cannot be out of Canada for more than six consecutive months, except that the month in which he so absents himself does not count.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext:
I agree with the minister as tion is that it does not seem to coincide with to what the intention is, but I am wondering what the minister has, I suggest in good faith,

been telling us during the discussion on second reading. As I understood him, he explained that one of the purposes of the bill was to permit a pensioner to be absent from Canada provided his absence did not exceed six months in a calendar year, but the situation that we are now finding embodied in this bill is not that he may be away for six months in a calendar year, but that he may not be away for more than six consecutive months in any twelve-month period?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext: No.

subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext: I think that is quite clear. Let us look at the hypothetical case mentioned by the hon. member for Vancouver East. He says, supposing a pensioner leaves Canada on the 1st of October and is absent in that particular calendar year-assuming he was not absent before October-for three months. In the next succeeding calendar year the minister says he must be back by March 31. Why is that? His absence in that calendar year may only be five months, if he returns at the end of May, but he certainly qualifies for not being absent for more than six months in that calendar year. Yet, as I understand this section, and the minister's interpretation is quite correct, it does not conform with his explanation and the person must come back so that the period of absence does not exceed six months in a twelve-month period. I want to point out that what we have been talking about during the debate has been a six months' absence in a calendar year.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext: He still does get a six months-absence in a calendar year. He may not be able to use it consecutively because, for argument's sake, being away the last three months of 1957, and not being able to be absent for a period of from four to six months, he must return by March 31. But he still has three more months; in fact, he has four; he has three plus the number of days he leaves in the preceeding month. He still has that period to go in 1958, although I admit he must return on March 31 because he has presumably been away a succeeding total of six months.

subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext: I wonder whether I might ask the minister this question. In view of the objection he raised to permitting unlimited absence from the country, what is the significance of that one day? Does he feel that because a pensioner is in a position where he might be able to travel back to Canadian soil for a period of 24 hours, by virtue of that fact he becomes eligible to draw pension?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext:
I think the whole thought behind the act is lost when that matter is brought into consideration. In the amendment we are saying-this is exactly the
Old Age Security Act
same as it was before except it is extended beyond six months-that a person cannot be absent any more than six months without having to return to Canada. All right, you say, for argument's sake, he can come back on January 31, having been away five months in the previous year. He can come back on January 31 and spend one day, leave again on February 1 and stay another five months. That is quite so. But at the same time we must have some limitation; and we choose to believe that the six-month period is actually the figure that should be used at this time.

subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext: The minister mentioned returning for one day. It would seem to me to be most unreasonable to say to a pensioner who was in Florida that he must pay his fare and all the expenses connected with such a trip in order to come back to Canada for one day. I ask that as a question. Would it seem reasonable to go to all of the expense to come here to Canada for one day which would qualify him for another three or four months in the south?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext: I think I understand what are the hon. member's thoughts, but in the present legislation there is provision that he could be away for three months-for argument's sake, say the last three months in 1957-and have to come back for one day before he can go away for another three months. This is simply extending the period. He can be away the last six months in 1957, come back for January 1 and be away for the first six months in 1958.

subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext: I do not question this provision being in the other bill but I still think it is unreasonable to expect an old age pensioner receiving $55 a month to return to Canada when the cost to come to Canada and return might be $200. To me it would seem to be unreasonable.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext: It would appear to me that a person who has been in Florida, can afford it. I am not saying that everybody who goes south is one who can afford it but I believe that quite a few people who go down there, shall I say, for six months and return for a day and go back for six months can probably afford to do it for the one day.

subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext: In line with the point raised by the hon. member over to my right,-I am not too sure which riding he represents-

subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext: Charlotte.

subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext:
-I think the wording of that particular section is a bit confusing. According to the explanation we have had

Old Age Security Act
from the minister, it means in essence that he cannot be away for more than six consecutive months.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext: That is right; that is the intent of it.

subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext: But it is a total of six months in one calendar year. Those are two entirely different meanings.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext: Will the hon. member repeat that question, please?

subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext:
The last line reads as follows:
-but not exceed a total of six months in any calendar year.
To take the wording literally it could mean that, in the hypothetical case that was raised, you could be away the last six months of this year, that is the last six months of 1957, and the first six months of 1958.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext: Provided that you returned for one day.

subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext: You would not be over six months in either of the two calendar years. But according to the explanation given by the minister, it means that you cannot be away for more than six consecutive months, regardless of which year it is.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext: That is not quite correct. The intent behind the amendment is that he cannot be away for more than six months. Mind you, he can be away for six months plus 29 days but that is the limit.

subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext: It seems clear from the legislation that if a pensioner decides to leave the country he cannot receive any moneys at all until he has returned. Then if there is any back pay owing, he gets it. It seems to me that if a person who is in receipt of old age pension, and who for that reason would not have any surplus supply of money, is going away say to a warmer climate, as for instance down to Florida, to live, and who needs this money from his pension, he should get it. How in the world is he ever going to be able to stay there if he receives none of his pension in the period between the time he leaves and the time he comes back? Surely it would not do him much good otherwise. He would never have an opportunity to save enough money to pay his expenses down there for six months. If he could do so, he would not need the pension. The very fact that he needs the pension, and needs it every month, seems to me to be sufficient reason to pay him on a monthly basis.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext:
I do not think we could do much about paying a pensioner when he was absent. If you continued to pay his cheque

during his absence he certainly would stay his full six months and there is no reason why he should not do so. By the amendment he is quite entitled to do that. But if he then did not come back to Canada we would be "out" the five months' cheques. We pay him his first month, the month in which he absents himself. From an administrative angle, it usually takes a few weeks to find out actually that the person is absent. Then the cheques are no longer mailed to him until he returns. It is true that maybe he has reason to have that money while he is still south in Florida or wherever it may be. If so, maybe he can save those cheques and use them to go south next year. But from an administrative angle I do not see how we could very well do otherwise. After all, we must protect our own situation.

subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext: The minister just pointed out a few moments ago that in all the time that pension has been in operation there were only something like 2,500 persons who had left and not returned.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext: That is one of the reasons; because this clause was in force.

subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext:
In all of the
time that this pension has been operative there have been only 2,500 who have not returned. But you are going to penalize the other pensioners because a few decided not to return. I really cannot think that is a good reason for penalizing all these other pensioners who are desirous of leaving the country, probably for health purposes, just because one or two may decide not to return. I think the government should give the matter further consideration and should make it possible for our old age pensioners to go away, enjoy their pension, then come back at the end of six months, and the next year they can go ahead and do the same thing. The pensioner will have a mighty hard time in saving up his pension cheques, even though he is living here, so as to have enough money put aside to go on a trip for six months.

subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext: I cannot see what argument the minister has for withholding the pension cheque merely because of fear that the man may decide not to some back. What difference does it make? If he does not come back at the end of six months, all right, he is cut off according to your amendment. But what possible reason is there for not paying him for that six months during which you say he is entitled to be out of the country? What administrative difficulty is there? Is it so difficult to put a stamp on a letter to the United States? I do not see how the minister can present any argument at all.

subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext: What I have to say is along the same line. In the first month that the old age pensioner goes outside of Canada he gets his cheque. According to the minister, he gets his cheque for the month that he goes out and he gets it as a right because it is his pension. But it is also his pension for six months. He only loses it as a right if he does not come back in six months but the first six months of his pension is a right. The five months is just as much a right as the first month so why cannot the pensioner get it? I am afraid the hon. minister is not making sense.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext: Well could I point out the following instance: if this person left the country ostensibly with the thought of returning in three to six months, as long as he is within the legal limit he is paid his cheque each month. However, if he decides to stay eight months then how could we recover the six months he had recevied?

subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext: Why should you want to recover the six months? That is his by right.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext: Because he owes us six months.

subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext: Why do you say he owes it to you; that is not your money it is his.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext: Not if he stays over the six months. That is not his right. He is not entitled to any one of those eight months he stays away over the six months.

subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext: What makes you say that, I do not see why?

subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, on this point; if a pensioner leaves Canada and goes to Arizona for reasons of health, spends six months down there and is unable to return because of his ill health, then that pensioner is being robbed of his right. He is being robbed of five months' pension. On the other hand if his health permits him to return to the country for one day then he can recover the amount of the cheques. This does not seem to me to be a very fair provision; it discriminates against persons who by virtue of their ill health are unable to return to Canada at the end of the six months period. If they have earned that pension by right and have decided for their own reasons to stay down there permanently, of course they are cut out and the treasury of Canada is no longer required to pay them any pensions for the balance of the time after the six months. In other words it seems to me that this provision is designed for one purpose only and that is to make sure those people who do not return are denied their pension
Old Age Security Act
cheques for five months. I can see no other reason for the wording of the provision as it now stands in the bill.

subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext: If you do not like it vote against it.

subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext: In reply, Mr. Chairman, the minister insinuated that any person who was able to go to Florida for six months could afford to go back and forth any time he wished.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext: No I did not.

subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext: Well I got that impression.

subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext: Do not put words into my mouth.

subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext: I have in mind a case of a gentleman and his wife whom I know very very well. He is a retired banker with a very small pension and has a very serious heart condition. His doctor advises him that he must not stay in a cold climate in winter time. This is the case I had in mind when I was speaking previously. Now for his wife and himself to go to Florida and for the matter of one day to be compelled to come back to Canada in order to qualify seems to me unreasonable. I do not question this was in the old act; I do not say it was not for one moment. However, even if it was in the old act I say that it is still wrong to compel a couple to come back to Canada, and put them to the expense of travelling back and forth simply to be here for one day in order to qualify for another three months down there. It does not seem reasonable to me at all.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext:
If I might point this out, my hon. friend's friend will at least have twice as long out of the country now as he did before without it being necessary for him to come back. As I mentioned earlier when I was closing the debate on second reading, there are probably certain things to be done, such as the possibility of giving consideration to pioneer Canadians who have lived all their lives in Canada and have given years of service, paid taxes and so on.
There may be other sections of the act which require consideration but at the moment we are simply changing these three fundamental clauses, these three fundamental points. We are raising the pension from $46 to $55; reducing the residence period requirement from 20 to 10 years, and increasing the period of permissible absence from three to six months. Now there may be other things to be considered and I am not saying there are not. There are the regulations with the province which I think should be examined but which I have not had an

Old Age Security Act
opportunity or quite frankly the time to examine. I have not been in office long enough but I am quite willing to consider these things as time goes on. However, as I say, at the moment we just have to accept the fact that these are the three fundamental changes which are required.

subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext:
The particular
change I have in mind is with respect to a person who would normally go away in say October or November. I am not thinking of the person who would go in January and stay away for six months or the next year-I think that is most reasonable-but I am thinking of the person who must be away during cold weather for reasons of health and leaves Canada for instance on the first of October; they are in Florida or some other country during October, November and December and they do not return to Canada until April 30.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext: They do not have to.

subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext: You said a few moments ago they could not have over six months.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext: If he returns on April 30 he is quite within his rights.

subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext: That is right, I do not question that.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext: If he leaves October 30 and returns April 30.

subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext: Well he has to come back on the first of April and be in Canada for one day and then go back for two more months. I still think it is unreasonable.

subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext: I think the hon. member has overlooked the fact that the spirit and intention of the act is that a person shall be allowed to stay out of Canada for six months. If he is going to come back to Canada for a day we would have to assume that he was merely coming back in a technical sense only.

subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext: To get his cheque.

subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext: To get around the provisions of the statute and in that case he would be coming back for a technical purpose but not to carry out the intention of the act. I would think in those circumstances if he felt like coming back he would be within his rights to do so, but it would be at his own expense.

subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext:
This is a departure from the principle established in the present section of the Old Age Security Act which reads as follows:
Where a pensioner absents himself from Canada, payment of his pension shall be suspended immediately following the payment for the month in

which he so absents himself, but may be resumed when the pensioner returns; and. where a pensioner returns to Canada within six months from the time he left Canada the pension upon being resumed may be also paid for a period of such absence not exceeding three months in any calendar year.
I understood that it was the practice that a pensioner could be away three months in one year or three months in the next or a total of six months and obtain his full pension upon return. I am of the opinion that this clause is more restrictive and departs from the principle which has been in effect since the act was first passed in this house.

subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I think under the old legislation there were cases where people were out of the country for a period of six months. I quite clearly recall an asthmatic case who went to Arizona in the last three months of the year and he stayed there until the end of March. I think upon his return he got his pension for the whole six months period. Now probably that was against the law so I should not reveal his name, but I still think that under the old act he could obtain his old age pension for three months in any calendar year.

subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, could I ask the minister if a person goes out of the country and stays away for eight months and then returns to Canada-assuming for medical reasons or something of that kind he had overstayed the six months period, coming back at the end of eight or nine months or even after a year-how long would he have to be in residence in Canada again before being entitled to further payments of the old age pension?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext: They are reinstated the month in which they return.

subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext: Can we assume that the calendar year is from January 1 to December 31 in any year?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext: A calendar year, yes.

subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext:
So a person, according to the
minister, can actually be away for seven months? In view of the fact that a person gets his pension at the end of September- the 28th or 30th-he can be away in October, November, December, January, February, returning here in March; there would be nothing to stop him doing that and leaving shortly afterwards. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext: That is correct.

subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext:
Why does the minister want
to keep these people from getting a pension? So far as I am concerned we are giving these people aged 70 and over a pension because they are 70 years of age. If they

are getting that pension because they are 70 years of age what the dickens difference does it make where they live?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext: No.

subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext:
Well, let us say it puts a
practical difficulty in the way of somebody staying out of the country for more than six months plus the additional month of departure, and it seems to me the minister ought to look at the clause and see whether it would not be possible to make the language clear so that somebody who perhaps has legitimate grounds for leaving the country during the winter months is not forced to go through what one hon. member referred to a moment ago as a technical return. It seems to me that the main provision is that the limitation should not exceed six months in any calendar year. I cannot see any difficulty whether he has his absences all together over a 12-month period or not, provided they do not exceed six months in any calendar year, but the procedure of going back every six or seven months to be able to establish his return to Canada and complete six months residence in that calendar year seems unjustified and farcical.

subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I rather agree with the hon. member who has just spoken, but for another reason. There seems to be an unfairness about this one-day return. For instance, let us take a person who lives in Toronto, who goes over to Buffalo and has to return for one day to establish his residence. It is no trouble for such a person to come back to Canada. But let us consider another person who lives here in Ottawa and who goes to Florida. That is a different matter; he has to return a long way just for the sake of one day to establish his residence. Some hon. members may say that it is a very small thing, but there is a distinction here, an unfairness as between one citizen and another.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext: They are all the same.

subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext:
No, a man who has to come back from Florida or from England is in a different position. Supposing a man goes to England. Does he have to come back for the 96698-48
Old Age Security Act
sake of one day? He does. So he is placed at very much of a disadvantage compared with another person who has to make a much shorter journey. As I say, there is unfairness between citizens, depending on how far they go away. It is all right to go across the line from Vancouver to Seattle and come back for a day, but a person who leaves Vancouver to go to England cannot come back for a day so easily.

subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext: Will the minister tell the house what is the value of causing an old age pensioner this extra expense in order to make a technical return of one day in order to qualify for another six month's eligibility for pension?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext: If you made it one year-if you made it two years, you would still need to have a return period, be it only one day. There was a return period prescribed under the three months legislation which had been in existence for some time. Now we are doubling that period of absence, but we still retain the one day requirement and I would venture to say that there are very few, if any, who contemplate returning for the one day. I venture to say that under this legislation a person leaving on October 1 can stay away till April 30, and I cannot imagine anything more reasonable than that.

Mr. Chairman, the explanatory note in the bill to this subsection reads as follows:
Where a pensioner absents himself from Canada, payment of his pension shall be suspended immediately following the payment for the month in which he so absents himself, but may be resumed when the pensioner returns:	and where the
pensioner returns to Canada within six months from the time he left Canada, the pension upon being resumed may also be paid for a period of such absence not exceeding three months in any calendar year.
As I read that it means that if a pensioner goes out of the country on October 1 and returns before the end of March he may receive his full six months pension with respect to the three months of the calendar year, October, November and December, and for the three months of January, February and March. So it was possible under the old

Old Age Security Act
legislation for a pensioner to be absent from the country for the full six months without having to return to Canada during that period.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext: He did, however, use up two years of rights; he could not go away the succeeding October and remain away without losing his benefits.

subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext:
I gather that the minister's main objection to paying an old age pensioner by the month while he is still away is the possibility that that pensioner may have no intention of returning. In other words, the pensioner might possibly have sold his house and decided to take up residence in another country to which the pension would be sent. I agree with the minister that in a case like that, that if a person had ended his domicile in this country, sold his house and made up his mind to five in another country, then the pension should not be paid.
On the other hand there might be cases of old age pensioners who own houses in this country and who fully intend to return. It seems to me there is a difference between the two situations. It seems to me it would be a comparatively easy thing for the minister to be assured that a pensioner intended to return. If he had property in this country he could give some form of guarantee that he intended to come back, otherwise the cost of that pension could be taken from the value of the house.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59

subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59

subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext: At least the department could get security from a pensioner who does own property in this country; it could go that far.

subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext:
I did say earlier, and it is quite true, that we do not pay a pensioner beyond the month in which he absents himself, because if he did happen to stay two or three months longer we would have the job of collecting. I am sure every hon. member of this house has had lots of letters from constituents from whom certain amounts have had to be collected, and they know how they are received. After all, collecting these sums is a very unpopular course. This particular course, however, does not seem to be unpopular among the beneficiaries. speechtext: Mr. Chairman, in order to overcome what seems to be the most serious objection to this clause, I wonder if the minister would consider amending it so that in the event a person was required to stay away for more than six months because of illness and then returned within a 12-month period intending to establish residence again he would be paid the full six months during which he was away. subtopic: GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT AND FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL EXPENDITURES ON OLD AGE PENSIONS, 1927-28 TO 1958-59
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I mentioned earlier that there were certain things to which I would be happy to give consideration and this is one of them but I do not feel this is the time to give that consideration. I think it has to be thought out very clearly and well.

Mr. Chairman, I think I can
appreciate something of the problem the minister faces from an administrative point of view, if for no other reason, which perhaps makes him hesitate at this time to consider making the pension payable as of right no matter where the pensioner may be. I think there are quite a number of administrative difficulties involved. I know some of them because I have had experience in administering pensions in the province and these problems would be ten times as great in the federal field.
I suppose we should be asking the former minister of national health and welfare concerning the philosophy behind the provision that exists requiring a return to Canada and withholding of the pension in the absence of the pensioner during the three or six month period during which he may be away because that was established by the Liberal administration and I am not in a position now to ask the former minister about that background.
I would certainly suggest to the new minister that in the next year or two he give consideration to the suggestion that has been made and see if the administrative difficulties can be overcome so the pension will be payable as of right no matter where the pensioner lives. I believe the minister said that approximately 2,500 pensioners had been cut off over the years in the past. It may be necessary to conduct some sort of survey to determine what has happened to them and what kind of problems were involved in their moving around.
If the minister would give an undertaking that he will give this matter consideration perhaps with a view to changing the act again at some not too distant future date I would be quite content to have the bill

put through in its present form. As I understand it, what we are doing here is simply extending the practice of the past but we are giving a six-month leave of absence rather than a three-month leave of absence. Under the old clause, as I understand it, a person could be away for six months without disqualifying himself but upon his return to the country all he could claim was a payment of pension for three months. Under the present scheme if he leaves for six months and then returns he can claim the whole of the six months under the regulations. It is an improvement, believe me.
If the minister cannot see his way clear to making the change that is requested now, if he will give me an undertaking that he will study the matter with a view to changing the system in the future I will, as I said, be prepared to let the bill pass in this form.

Mr. Chairman, I think the minister has already made it clear that the consideration involved in this matter of not carrying on the pension payment during the period the pensioner is absent is not one of administrative difficulty. Apparently he has made it clear that he is prepared to deny the rights of pensioners to be absent from Canada for more than the month in which they go away as a matter of right. I wonder if the minister could give us an idea of what he estimates would be the drain on the treasury of Canada if that period of absence were granted as a right and the pension payments were continued up to the period which he proposes of six months.
I think it has become obvious during this discussion that the whole impact of these restrictions is going to rest upon the people who depend primarily upon the old age pension. The problem of coming back for a day for a week or longer is not a serious matter to the person who has other means but this is not the case with the person who because of health or family connections wants to reside outside of Canada and is dependent almost entirely upon the pension. Such people are really caught in the bite with regard to this matter.
It seems to me it is all very well for the minister to say this is a matter to which he will give consideration in the future. We all recognize that the minister has not been in office very long as yet and there may be a great many matters to which he has not had an opportunity of giving adequate study, but at the same time I would point out that this particular matter is not a new one for this house. It has been the subject of pretty

Old Age Security Act

It seems to me that having gone as far as he has the minister might have gone one little step further, unless he can convince us it is going to make such a great drain upon the treasury that the matter of extending this right would bankrupt the government of Canada.
